CHAPTER 20: TEACHERS WHO FANNED THE FLAMES

Tuesday afternoon, May 1979, ten days before the Battle. Bob Wentworth had the jazz band in a horseshoe — seventeen kids on folding chairs in the cinder-block room off the east wing, ballast buzz in the fluorescents, dust motes turning in the late light that came slantwise through the one high window. The posters on the wall were a small argument he had been having with himself since 1962. Ellington at the Blue Note. Miles in shadow, the Harmon mute at his lips. Bernstein with his baton down. A tasteful cross-section, or that was what he had told his wife when he tacked them up. A man's divided loyalties in frames.

The Yamaha upright stood against the long wall, lid open, middle C pitted where ten years of middle-school hands had found it first. Nick's Marshall practice amp sat on a chair by the piano, not plugged in yet, the cord coiled on top with the precision of a boy who owned one cord. Music stands at seventeen different heights. A broken maraca on the shelf above the tuba case, the handle snapped off at the bead, which Wentworth kept for reasons he could not articulate. The room smelled of old valve oil and floor wax.

He had the photograph in his drawer. He had been thinking about it all period.

"Put the scales away," he said. He set a stapled two-page chart on each of their music stands. "Brubeck. 'Take Five.' Nick, Jackie — just you two. The rest of you listen."

Seventeen heads came up.

Nick was by the amp, not looking at the piano. Jackie was already on the bench, not looking at the amp. They had not spoken, Wentworth knew, since October. Two Aprils of careful air between them in a building with two hundred and forty feet of corridor.

"Mr. Wentworth," Nick said. He had not picked up the guitar. "I don't think —"

"Five-four," Wentworth said. "One, two, three, four, five. The off-balance is the point. You lean into it. Just see."

Jackie put his hands on the keys. Nick, because there was nowhere else for his hands to go, plugged in.

---

The left hand came first. D, E-flat, F — ostinato, walking — the Brubeck bass figure the way the record had it, Jackie's fingers finding the shape clean on the first pass because classical training had given him the 5/4 the way it had given him everything, for free. The ostinato settled into the room like a heartbeat that had decided to come in a pattern nobody's body expected. One, two, three, four, five. One, two, three, four, five.

Nick listened for four bars. He found the crack between the four and the five and he put a bent blue note in it. Low on the neck. Not loud. The string was slightly flat and he let it be flat. Another bar of listening, and then he threaded the second phrase, longer, letting the time signature lean him sideways and catching himself on a chord, and the chord was not a Brubeck chord, it was an Aerosmith chord, and it sat down in Jackie's ostinato like it had been waiting there.

Jackie's right hand came in above it. Not flourish — restraint. A single high note held, then a run, then held again. He was leaving Nick room.

Nick stepped into the room Jackie left him.

For thirty seconds it was a working thing. The off-balance found its center the way a bicycle finds its center, not by stopping the wobble but by leaning into it. In the horseshoe one kid — Brian Castellano, second chair trumpet — stopped chewing his gum and his jaw hung half-open and he did not remember to close it. In the corner, on flute, Patty Lally from Sudbury Southeast had been humming something of her own under her breath the whole period, a Fleetwood Mac melody she didn't know she was humming, and the hum was going now, quiet, underneath the 5/4 like a third voice the room had not been asked to provide. She lowered the flute to her lap. She did not lift it again.

Wentworth did not move. He was not sure he was breathing. The ballast buzz was the only thing in the building that did not know what was happening in the room.

---

The door whooshed on its hydraulic hinge.

Don Gould came in the way Don Gould came in — Northeastern coffee mug in the left hand, jeans, sleeves rolled to the elbow, wool tie loose at the collar, the AP American History grin he wore on days he thought he was going to teach somebody something. He stopped in the doorway long enough to register the music, which was still happening, the ostinato walking under him, and then he smiled wider.

Patty Lally's hum stopped.

"You know what this is?" Gould said, loud, over the music that was still going. "This is the Lincoln-Douglas debates, right here."

Nick's hand came off the strings.

Jackie's ostinato carried one more bar on its own, alone, the D-E-flat-F figure with nothing on top of it, and then Jackie's left hand stopped too, the last note hanging and dying into the ballast buzz.

---

Nick set his pick down on the amp. He set it down carefully, because if he had not set it down carefully he would have thrown it.

"We were playing music," he said.

Gould was still smiling. "Right, but — the tension, Nick, the tension between —"

"Between the kids who matter and the kids who don't." Nick stood. The strap caught on the music stand; the stand went over; the Brubeck chart went under a chair. He didn't pick it up. "Between the kids whose parents donate the new risers and the kids whose parents die in a trailer the company blames on the guy who was inside it."

Gould's smile did a thing. It did not go away. It got confused at the edges.

"You want a lesson?" Nick was unplugging the cord now. His hands knew the cord. His hands did not need his face to do it. "Fine. Here's your lesson. Jackie's going to Juilliard or Yale or wherever. I'm going to work construction like my dad. Maybe die quick like him too. That American enough?"

In the horseshoe, Patty Lally looked down at the silver keys of the flute in her lap. Her thumb moved on the G key and stopped. Something in her face went somewhere it had not been before.

"Nick." Jackie's voice was small. He had not stood up. His hands had come off the keyboard and were flat on his thighs.

"What."

"Don't."

"Don't what. Don't say it in front of people? Your dad said it in front of people. *These boys don't understand boundaries.* On the bridge. In front of my friends. In front of me."

Jackie's hands came off his thighs and went back to the keys and did not press anything. The fluorescent buzzed. One of the tubes up near the door was going; it ticked twice, a small electric tick, and then buzzed again.

"I was trying to avoid this." Jackie's voice had gone quieter, not louder. The precision was starting to crack at the edges the way it did when he was tired. "I thought maybe we could get through one week without —"

"Without what. Without you stepping aside like a good little prince on a wooden bridge. Without your Queen covers being you slumming with real people."

"Slumming." Jackie said the word like it was a small heavy object somebody had handed him. He did not look up. His breath came in once and did not come out evenly.

He stood. The piano bench scraped on the tile, the short ugly sound of oak on waxed linoleum, and the sound was loud because the room had gone so quiet around it. He shut the fallboard. He did not slam it. He set it down the way his mother set a china cup down.

"See you Friday," Jackie said.

That was all. He walked out. The door went on its hinge and the hinge whooshed and closed on the soft seal.

Nick was still holding the cord.

---

Wentworth got them out of the room. He did not remember, afterward, what he said to do it — some sentence with the word *dismissed* in it, probably — but the seventeen chairs emptied, folders under arms, and the last kid out was Patty Lally, who paused at the door with the flute case under her elbow and looked back once at the piano bench and then was gone.

The door closed on its seal.

The ballast buzz was still the only sound.

Wentworth walked past the Yamaha, past Nick's amp with its coiled cord, past the Brubeck chart under the chair, and went around behind the piano to the stand where the trumpet had been since September, in its black case, and had not been out of its case in fourteen months. He opened the case. The felt lining had gone bald at the bell end. The valve oil bottle on the inside of the lid was three-quarters down, where he had left it.

He took the horn out. He set the mouthpiece in. The mouthpiece was cold. He wet his lips. He raised the horn. The ring on the bell said *Bach Stradivarius 37* in the same small script it had said it in at Jordan Hall in March of 1958.

He blew one note.

It was not a good note. It was an F, and the F sagged under his breath because the embouchure had gone and the lip had gone and the air had gone, and the note came out of the bell and went nowhere. Nobody heard it. The room ate it.

He set the horn back in the case. He closed the case.

He sat down on the piano bench Jackie had left.

**END CHAPTER 20**

CHAPTER 19: GRACE LOSES HER GRACE

Grace Johnson carried the two pots the way she had carried them for twenty-three years: regular in her right hand, orange collar on the glass; decaf in her left, brown collar. Dr. Taub drank decaf. Had drunk decaf since 1956, the year she started and he was still new to his practice, thirty-two and just back from Korea with his wire-framed glasses and a cardigan his wife had knit him and a bedside manner he had not yet grown into. Grace went to his table with the brown-collared pot already tilted, because at Friendly's on Route 20 you did not ask Dr. Taub which coffee he wanted. You poured the decaf and you said good morning, Dr. Taub, and you did not stand any longer at his booth than the pour required.

Booth twelve was the booth by the window. The window looked out on the parking lot and the Route 20 traffic going east toward Wayland, and the Impala in the second row and Grace's wood-paneled '67 station wagon in the first. Above her, the fluorescent flickered the way it had flickered since Tom Andrews had taken over in '71 and failed to fix it. The ice cream case against the back wall hummed through its blue light. MINT CHOCOLATE CHIP, the little cardboard flag said in its Friendly's-green script, stuck into a tub gone frost-bristled at the edges. At booth seven a kid was working on a Jim Dandy with a long spoon. A booth down from him, two cops split a Fishamajig basket. The air was what the air at Friendly's always was — fryer oil laid over coffee laid over the bleach on the rag in her apron pocket.

Dr. Taub had the Sudbury Weekly folded open to page three. The picture on page three was Nick, head down over the Les Paul copy in the music-room shot they had run with the WBCN story, the same shot that had been on WBCN's newsbrief last Thursday when the PTA fight went statewide for eleven seconds. Dr. Taub was a man of seventy now. The suit jacket hung over the back of the booth. Under it he wore the same kind of cardigan he had worn when she was twelve and his wife had been Ruth Lindstrom, in the L-S class of '55 two years behind her, and the two of them had sat at the same lunch table in a cafeteria that did not exist anymore. He did not remember that. He had never needed to.

"Grace," he said. He did not look up from the paper. "I've been reading about this Battle."

"Yes, Dr. Taub." She poured. Brown collar. Steady.

"I worry about these boys. Yours. The Marsh boy." He touched the photograph with his index finger, the way he touched a chart. "The competition sets them up. Expectations. Talent alone — you know — it takes training. Connections. Most of these kids are going to be disappointed."

There was a small brown stain on the lapel of his cardigan he had not noticed. Coffee, or something coffee-adjacent, from a morning older than today. She noticed it.

"Disappointed," she said.

"I delivered that boy, Grace." He said it the way a man lays down a trump. "I delivered Nick in March of '62 at Emerson. I'm not against him. I'm *for* realism."

The pot in her left hand was half full. She did not set it down. She did not slam it. She held it.

"My son has been playing guitar since he was eight."

She said it the way she would have said, *the oven's on.* And she was looking, as she said it, past Dr. Taub's cardigan shoulder, through the window of booth twelve, and the late-morning sun on the parking lot caught the chrome handle of the station wagon in a flash she would not have let herself notice any other day — the handle of her third car, the wagon she'd bought used in '74 after Dan's truck needed a clutch, and for a single beat the light on the chrome was the light off a different door handle on a different car in a different driveway a long time ago, and she swallowed around it and did not let her voice shake.

"He practices every day in the garage his father built. He's won every talent show he's entered since he was nine. WBCN called my house. Not his. Mine. And you're drinking decaf in my section at eleven in the morning and telling me he's going to be disappointed."

Dr. Taub opened his mouth.

"Enjoy your coffee, Dr. Taub."

She moved to booth seven. Jim Dandy kid. "You need anything, honey?" He shook his head. She moved to the cops. Refilled them both. Regular. Orange collar. She did not look back at booth twelve. She did not need to. The whole dining room had gone a shade quieter, the way a pond goes quiet when something has fallen in it.

---

Tom Andrews was forty-eight and had been the Friendly's manager on Route 20 for eight of those years. His office was a cinder-block closet behind the walk-in, with a gray metal desk, a swivel chair with duct tape on the arm, a bank calendar from Middlesex Savings still turned to March. He had grown up on Horse Pond Road. He had poured concrete on the same crew as Dan Johnson for two summers in the early sixties. He had been at the funeral.

"Sit down, Grace."

"I'll stand, Tom."

"Sit down."

She sat.

He did not look at her while he said the sentences his job required him to say. Professionalism. Customer relations. The uniform meaning something. The word *uniform* was doing work in his mouth that the word was not built for. He finished. He set both hands flat on the desk.

"Fifteen more cents an hour."

"Thanks, Tom."

"Get back to work, Grace."

"Yes, sir."

She stood. She untied and retied the apron. Her name tag had come loose on the left pin; she straightened it. GRACE, in the raised plastic letters, and under it MANAGER, and the small gold foil star the company had sent in February. She went back out to the floor.

---

He came in at four-ten, through the glass door with the Friendly's-cone sticker on it, and he stood by the register with his L-S jacket on and his hands in his pockets and his weight on his right leg. Dan had stood like that. Waiting for Grace to finish a shift, Dan had always tilted the weight off the bad knee, and Nick had never once in his seventeen years been told to copy the stance, and there it was. Grace saw it from booth four, where she was wiping syrup off a formica edge, and went still for a half-second and then kept wiping.

He crossed to her.

"Mom."

"It's fine, Nick."

"I heard."

"You deserve a chance."

"You didn't have to do that."

"Yes, I did."

She folded the rag. She did not look at him right away. When she did, his face had the Friendly's sign in the window of it — the cursive neon red reflected on the lens of his reading glasses, which were her reading glasses, which he had grabbed off the counter when he came in, and he did not know he was wearing them. She almost said so. She didn't.

"Wait on the bench by the door," she said. "Two minutes."

He waited on the bench by the door. She took the apron off in the back. She hung it on the hook that had her name taped above it in Tom's block print. She clocked out. She walked past the ice cream case with its blue light and the mint chocolate chip and the Jim Dandy sign and out through the glass door, and Nick stood up off the bench and walked out beside her, and above them the Friendly's sign in its ice-cream-cone cursive threw red over the hood of the station wagon and red over the shoulders of her polyester and red, a softer red, over the side of Nick's face. Eight days to the Battle.

They did not speak in the parking lot. He opened the driver's side for her the way Dan used to. She got in. He walked around to the passenger side. For a moment, before he opened his door, he stood in the lot with his hand on the roof of the wagon and looked back at the diner where his mother had just, without once saying the word, defended him in front of the doctor who had delivered him and the town that had watched her serve coffee for twenty-three years.

Then he got in, and she started the engine, and they went home up Route 20 with the red sign fading in the rearview and the spring light going long over the Cavicchio fields.

**END CHAPTER 19**

CHAPTER 18: THE TOWN WEIGHS IN

By the last week of April the town had made up its mind without anyone calling a vote.

Grace Johnson felt it first at the Star Market on Route 20 with a ten-pound sack of Maine potatoes in the crook of her arm. The plastic netting was cutting a red line across the inside of her elbow and she was waiting her turn at register three. The cashier — Donna, the daughter of the older Donna who had worked this same register since Grace was a girl — rang the potatoes through without looking at them.

"Nick nervous?"

"He's fine."

"My Tommy says the whole school's picking sides."

"Tommy's a sophomore."

"Still."

She took her change in quarters because Donna was out of ones, and on the way to the door the pharmacist behind the raised counter of the Osco lifted two fingers and called across the shampoo aisle — *tell him good luck for us, Grace* — the way he might have said it at a wake. Grace lifted two fingers back. She did not break stride.

She put the potatoes in the back of the wagon and stood for a second with her hand on the tailgate, looking at the parking lot. A boy maybe nine years old was pushing a line of carts toward the corral. Two old men were talking by the ice machine. Nothing was happening. Everything was happening.

---

Tuesday was her one day a week off from Friendly's and she sat at the Sudbury Diner on Route 20 the way she had sat there every Tuesday for six years, in the back booth where the vinyl was split along the seam and the crack had been mended with a piece of black electrical tape. The Globe was open in front of her. The Red Sox had lost to the Yankees again.

The voices came over the top of the newsprint.

*— real talent versus noise —*

*— Marsh boy's had lessons since he was six —*

*— heart doesn't win anything —*

She did not look up. She turned the page. A Bradlees ad for lawn chairs.

"Grace."

Mary Murphy sat down across from her without asking. Mary's husband drove for the post office and had a brown Chevy Impala with a dented right-rear quarter panel where he'd backed it into the mailbox at the Fairbank Road turnaround in March and never gotten it fixed, and you could see the car from the diner window right now, the dent catching the late sun. Their son Stephen played bass in Nick's band.

"He holding up?"

"He's fine."

"Stephen says they're in the garage six hours a night."

"Something like that."

Mary leaned in. Her voice dropped half an inch. "Frank at the barber shop's got a pool going."

"On what."

"On Nick."

"Jesus, Mary."

"My Dennis put ten dollars down."

The waitress came by with the pot. The button over her apron pocket was a white circle with red letters — **WBCN 104.1 — THE ROCK OF BOSTON** — with the peace-sign logo underneath, slightly crooked where the pin had gone in a dozen times. She topped Grace's cup without asking, topped Mary's, moved on to the booth behind.

"The Weekly ran it again yesterday," Mary said. "Front page."

Grace had seen it. The photograph was Nick in the garage, three-quarters to the light from the open door, Dan's tools outlined in black marker on the pegboard behind him and the 1975 Aerosmith calendar hanging exactly where it had hung for four years. *BATTLE OF THE BANDS: TWO STUDENTS, TWO WORLDS, ONE STAGE.* Sponsored in part, the last paragraph said, by WBCN-FM. The reporter had called three times before Grace picked up. She had given him seven sentences.

"Dr. Marsh didn't like it," Mary said. "My neighbor works in the office. He called the school. Said they were turning a talent show into class warfare." Mary put quotes around *class warfare* with two fingers on each hand.

Grace sipped her coffee.

"There's a PTA meeting Thursday night. Emergency session. He's going to try to cancel it."

Grace set the cup down.

"Cancel it."

"Postpone until fall. For the kids' own good. You know the song."

"The Battle's in two weeks."

"I know."

Grace looked across the booth at Mary Murphy. Fifteen years they had lived three streets apart. Fifteen years of Little League and parent-teacher nights and hand-me-down snowsuits. Mary's house was the same house as Grace's house — the same square of chain-link, the same sagging gutter over the back door — paid for one month at a time.

"I work Thursday," Grace said.

"Get it off."

"I can't."

"Grace."

"I'll get it off."

---

Thursday the Lincoln-Sudbury library smelled the way it had smelled in 1953 — lemon oil the librarian rubbed into the oak shelves every morning before the doors opened, varnish gone amber on the long card catalog by the reference desk, paper and dust and the faint electric warmth of the fluorescent tubes overhead. Grace had checked out a copy of *The Yearling* from these shelves in the spring she turned fifteen. She had forgotten until she stepped through the door and the smell came up and found her.

She did not think about it for long. She did not have time.

The room was full. The good oak chairs filled first, in rows facing the librarian's desk; then the metal folding chairs along the walls, scraped out of the supply closet; then parents standing in the doorway. Someone's baby was fussing at the back. The PA system crackled once — a cough of static — and went quiet. Principal Sargent sat at the front with his hands flat on a legal pad, the expression of a man who had not asked for this.

Grace came straight from work. She stood along the side wall next to a radiator that was ticking. Brown polyester uniform. *GRACE — MANAGER* over her left breast. The smell of fryer oil was on her whether she wanted it to be or not.

Dr. Marsh sat in the front row with his wife. Blazer, gray slacks, the easy posture of a man who had sat on a dozen nonprofit boards and knew how long to wait before raising a hand. He raised it.

"Thank you, Brad." He used the first name the way a man uses a key he has been given. "I think we all want the same thing. And I think we all know that this — competition — has become something none of us signed up for. Students skipping class. Arguments in the hallway. A newspaper poll asking seventeen-year-olds to pick a side as if this were a selectman's race."

Around the room, heads moved. A woman two chairs over pressed her lips together and nodded once. A man in a Red Sox windbreaker folded his arms across his chest.

"What troubles me most," Dr. Marsh said, "is that we have let a talent show turn into a referendum. On what, I'll let each of you decide. I am asking this board to postpone the Battle of the Bands until the fall, when cooler heads —"

Grace said, "Excuse me."

Her voice was not loud. It carried because the room had gone still for it.

Principal Sargent turned his head. "Mrs. Johnson."

She walked down the center aisle between the oak chairs. She was conscious of her sneakers on the waxed floor and the fryer smell coming off her uniform and the fact that she had not had a sentence ready when she left her car. She stopped at the front. She did not go behind the little lectern Sargent had set up. She put her right hand on the back of the nearest oak chair and gripped it. Her knuckles went white around the wood.

Dr. Marsh, half-risen, sat back down. His right hand lifted and moved to his left breast pocket as if to take something out of it. The pocket was empty. His hand rested there a second and then came down to his knee.

"I'm Grace Johnson," Grace said. "Nick's mother. I work at Friendly's. I worked a double today."

She stopped. The coffee she had drunk in the car an hour ago had gone cold in her mouth and she worked it down once before she went on.

"Dr. Marsh is right. This stopped being about a talent show. Our kids didn't do that. We did."

A chair creaked at the back.

"My son plays a twenty-five-dollar guitar in a garage his father built. His father is dead. He works Saturdays at a body shop for strings. Two weeks from now he gets to stand on a stage and play for five hundred dollars and a day in a studio. That's not nothing. That's the whole thing."

She looked at Dr. Marsh. She did not make a speech of it.

"You want to postpone it until fall. Fall is when Jackie goes to conservatory. Fall is when my son is fixing cars."

Someone in the metal folding chairs said, quiet, *that's right.*

Grace's hand was still on the oak chair. She could feel the grain under her thumb. The baby at the back had stopped fussing.

"Let them play," she said. "Win or lose. Let them play."

She did not walk back to the side wall. She walked down the aisle and out the double doors and into the parking lot. The sodium lights had come on. Her hands were shaking by the time she got the key into the door of the wagon, and she sat behind the wheel with both hands on it for a minute before she turned the ignition.

She drove home down Route 20 past the lit sign of the Star Market and the dark sign of the feed store, and the speedometer needle sat an even five miles over the limit the whole way, because that was the speed she drove.

---

Mary called at ten-forty.

"Forty-two to eleven."

"Alright."

"Grace. You should've seen his face."

"I'm glad."

"Brad called the vote five minutes after you walked out. Wasn't even close."

"Alright, Mary."

"That was the bravest —"

"I have to be there at five-forty."

A pause on the line.

"Get some sleep," Mary said.

"You too."

Grace set the receiver back in the cradle of the rotary phone on the kitchen wall, and the small internal click of the hanger-bar dropping into place was the last sound in the house. The kitchen clock ticked. Upstairs the garage amp was off. She stood with her hand still on the receiver for a second, then she turned off the kitchen light and went up the stairs in the dark the way she had gone up them ten thousand times, her right hand on the banister where the varnish had worn thin to the grain under her father's hand and her own.

**END CHAPTER 18**

CHAPTER 17: JACKIE'S WORLD

The Howard Miller grandfather clock in the hall struck six-thirty and the Marshes sat. That was how it worked in the house on Maple Street — the clock began to strike, and by the fourth tone the four of them were at the table with napkins across their laps. The clock finished behind them. The tick kept going. Jackie had measured the tick once on a metronome he'd borrowed from the Curtis music room. Seventy-two beats per minute. Andante. Which was also the pace his father walked down a hospital hallway.

The table was mahogany, the grain running the long way, a single dark whorl near the head like a water-stain from someone else's grief. The silver had belonged to Eileen's father — W.B.H. engraved at the shaft end of each knife and fork, W. B. Hollister, a Beacon Hill man who had lived long enough to see his daughter marry a psychiatrist and long enough to let her have the forks. The candlesticks on the sideboard were his too. The money in this house had come from her side. Jackie had worked that out by eleven without anyone telling him.

Eileen brought the plates in from the kitchen on a tray. Chicken piccata. The capers sat in a thin gold sauce that caught the chandelier light and threw it back in small wet stars. Lemon. Butter. The chicken pounded thin as stationery and laid in overlapping half-moons. Against the long wall, between the windows and the sideboard, stood the walnut upright Jackie had never seen his father touch. Its ivories had yellowed. Its music stand held an open hymnal nobody sang out of. Above the upright hung a Rothko reproduction — two rectangles of deep red over deep black, tasteful and just off-center in a way that pretended not to be. The brass switchplate beside the door was polished Tuesdays.

"Jackson received his acceptance letter," Eileen said. She had said it twice already today, once to Mrs. Caldwell on the phone and once to Jackie in the kitchen. This was the performance. "Early admission. The Juilliard School. Full scholarship."

"Congratulations," Elizabeth said.

"Thank you," Jackie said.

Dr. Marsh set down his wine glass. The base touched the mahogany and made a small definite sound. "We're proud, Jackson." He cut a piece of the chicken with the same clean motion he'd used for twenty years. "I assume you'll keep with Mr. Holloway through graduation. No reason to let the hands go soft before fall."

"Of course."

"The Jordan Hall recital is April twentieth. The program coordinator telephoned on Thursday. They want the Nocturne in E-flat. Opus nine, number two. The one you took to Tanglewood."

Jackie put his fork down. The capers moved in their sauce.

April twentieth was three weeks out from the Battle of the Bands at the high school auditorium. Three weeks of Chopin in the cathedral acoustic of Jordan Hall, then a week and a half of Freddie Mercury's gospel choir stacked over A-flat. Andante, then that other thing. He could feel both pieces in different parts of his body. The Chopin was in the first and fourth fingers of his left hand, the turn and the lift. The Queen was in his throat.

"I can do both," Jackie said.

"Do both."

"The recital and the competition."

Dr. Marsh looked at him. Not unkindly. That was the thing — the look never went unkind. "The recital draws reviewers from the Globe, Jackson. Faculty from the Conservatory. That is a career. The other — "

"Is also real."

The words came out faster than he'd meant them. The word *real* sat in the air with the capers and the lemon and the tick of the clock in the hall.

Jackie watched his father's hand go to the wine glass.

Dr. Marsh's fingers closed around the stem. His thumb rode down to where the stem met the base, and on the word *beneath* — which he had not yet spoken but was about to — his first three fingertips curled in, very slightly, in a shape the stem did not require, a shape the stem could not possibly have asked for. It was the shape of a hand laid across three strings and pressed. It lasted the breath before the word and was gone when the word came.

"Jackson. This is a high school competition. Sponsored by a rock station. It is beneath your level."

Jackie did not answer.

Eileen's smile did the thing it did, the tightening at the inside corners. "Sweetheart. Your father only means — "

"May I be excused?" Elizabeth said.

"Finish your beans," Eileen said.

Elizabeth ate three beans the way a person counts steps on a staircase she does not want to be climbing. Then she folded her napkin and left. Her shoes on the stairs did not quite slam and did not quite not-slam. Her door closed. The clock ticked.

"We'll discuss this later," Dr. Marsh said. "When everyone has had time."

"Yes, sir."

Jackie finished the chicken because he had been raised to finish the chicken. Under the table the first and fourth fingers of his left hand walked the Nocturne on his thigh through the denim, andante, seventy-two. His throat remembered the Queen chorus on its own without being asked.

---

Upstairs, the hallway carpet deadened everything. Jackie's bedroom was at the end. The door closed behind him with the soft brass click of a door in a house where doors were hung correctly.

The Chopin was already on the music stand by the Steinway — the Henle edition, E-flat major, Opus 9 No. 2, the *Andante* marking at the top in the engraver's careful italic. On the shelf over the desk sat the Tanglewood trophy: a brass treble clef on a walnut base, *Tanglewood Young Artists Competition — First Prize — Piano — 1977*. On the desk, weighted half under the trophy of the younger competition, lay the Juilliard envelope. Cream laid paper. The return address printed in the school's clean serif: *The Juilliard School, 144 West 66th Street, New York, NY 10023*. It had been opened with a letter knife along the top edge, not torn.

Jackie sat on the bed. He did not go to the piano yet.

In the bottom drawer of the desk, under a stack of old Curtis programs, lay a small Panasonic transistor the size of a deck of cards. Fresh batteries. Tuned to 104.1, the dial taped there with a strip of electrical tape so it would not wander off WBCN in the night. His father did not permit rock stations in the house. Jackie listened at a whisper after midnight with the radio under the pillow, and Maxanne's voice came through it low and bourbon-slow and went somewhere in his head and stayed there.

A knock on the door. "It's me."

"Come in."

Elizabeth was thirteen and small for it. She wore her plaid uniform skirt and one sock pulled up to the knee and one sock rolled down at the ankle, the asymmetry absolutely deliberate. She sat on the bed cross-legged. Her thumbnail found a loose thread in the chenille bedspread and began to work at it — a slow careful plucking, the way their mother worried the pearls at her throat during the Globe crossword.

"You're going to do the Battle of the Bands anyway," she said.

"Yeah."

"Even though he'll lose his mind."

"Yeah."

Her thumbnail kept at the thread. "Is it because of Nick Johnson?"

Jackie's hand went still on the bedspread. The Juilliard envelope shifted half an inch under his elbow, paper whispering against paper. A small physical thing. He felt it without moving.

"It's complicated," he said.

"You guys used to be best friends."

"Yeah."

"What happened? I always wanted to know but I was afraid to ask."

Jackie looked past her at the window. Maple Street at dusk. The six houses he could see from his bed sat at the same setback from the curb — twenty-two feet; he had paced it once. The streetlights were coming on in a sequence, the first at the Caldwells', then the Petersons', then the Schiffs', each one striking a second behind the last, a small orderly arpeggio of sodium glow. The hedges were clipped to the same height. The mailboxes stood at the same angle. Somebody down the block was pulling into a driveway in a Buick the color of a Buick.

"We grew up," Jackie said. "People change."

"That's what adults say when they don't want to explain things."

The corner of his mouth moved. A breath caught and came out as nothing.

"Yeah," he said. "It is."

Elizabeth pulled the loose thread another eighth of an inch. She did not look at him. The thread came free in her thumbnail and she rolled it into a small tight bead between finger and thumb.

"I heard you practicing last night," she said. "After they went to bed. That Queen song. The one."

"'Somebody to Love.'"

"You sounded different."

"Different how."

She thought about it. She thought about it a long time. The clock downstairs kept its andante. The sodium lamps on Maple Street came on in their order.

"Like you actually cared about the notes," she said, "instead of just hitting them right."

The silence held. Jackie did not fill it. Elizabeth did not fill it. The Juilliard envelope lay under his elbow with its Manhattan address pressed into the paper. The silence took up the space where the next thing should have gone, and then it took up a little more, and neither of them broke it.

"Don't tell Dad," Jackie said at last.

"Obviously."

She stayed a minute longer. Then she got up and went to the door with her one sock up and her one sock down, and she paused with her hand on the knob.

"Jackie. I hope you win the other one. Not because of Juilliard. Because last night you sounded like a person."

The door closed behind her.

---

Jackie sat where he was until the hallway carpet stopped conducting her footsteps. Then he went to the desk.

The Curtis talent-show photograph stood in a small silver frame next to the lamp. May 1975. Two thirteen-year-old boys on the auditorium stage — Jackie in a clip-on tie, Nick in a flannel shirt with the cuffs rolled — a plywood trophy held between them at chest height, their free arms around each other's shoulders. Nick's grin had a tooth missing. Jackie's grin had both arms of both boys in it. They had figured out, in that photograph, the only thing either of them had ever figured out.

He held it a long time. The desk lamp threw his own reflection faintly on the glass — the fifteen-year-old face over the thirteen-year-old face, the new one looking down at the old one through his own ghost.

He opened the bottom desk drawer. He laid the photograph face down on top of the stack of old programs and closed the drawer.

The house was quiet. The piano was not playing itself.

Jackie crossed to the Steinway and sat and set the Henle edition square on the stand and put his hands on the keys. The fingers found the E-flat chord at the top of the page without being asked, the left hand low and open, the right lifting for the andante. His throat, on its own, remembered the Queen chorus and did not sing it.

He began to play the Chopin.

**END CHAPTER 17**

CHAPTER 22: JACKIE'S REHEARSAL

May 14, 1979. Early evening. Eighteen hours to the Battle and Jackie Marsh was alone in the basement on Maple Street, running the intro of "Bohemian Rhapsody" in B-flat because his left hand had asked for it the second he sat down.

The room had been finished the summer he turned fourteen. Foam panels on the walls, the two-inch studio kind — white once, now going yellow at the glued edges the way a paperback goes yellow on a south-facing shelf. A Shure SM58 stood on a boom stand at the center of the floor, black grille, the XLR running in a clean loop to the four-track against the wall — a Tascam, four little red LED indicators glowing dim as pilot lights in a kitchen at night. Against the long wall, the upright. A 1920s Baldwin, its walnut case gone plum-dark at the corners, its ivory top keys chipped in two places from a thumbnail that had been Eileen's mother's in 1931 in a parlor on Beacon Hill. The Steinway lived upstairs in the good light. The Baldwin lived down here with the amps. That had been decided early.

Jackie played the opening six bars and let them stop themselves. His right thumb rested on the D. The ballast in the overhead fluorescent made its small even buzz and the foam drank it.

He had heard about Grace Johnson's speech at Friendly's. Everyone in Sudbury had heard about it by Wednesday. The knowledge sat in his chest the way a swallowed pill sits before it starts to go down.

---

They came in at six-thirty the way they always came in, Tuesday-Thursday-Saturday, the Crown Jewels coming down the side stairs in the order of their cars.

Ace Callahan first, because Ace always came first — the Premier kit was already set up down here, red-sparkle shells, the kick drum head with the black CROWN JEWELS decal he'd rubbed on with a pencil and a sheet of Letraset. He sat and ran a double-stroke roll on the snare without a word and the foam ate most of it. Max Wesslen came in behind him with the Fender Precision — black body, rosewood neck, the bass his father had bought him at E. U. Wurlitzer in the Back Bay for his sixteenth birthday — and plugged into the Ampeg cabinet and played four notes of the Queen bassline to warm the hand.

Elizabeth came last, because she lived upstairs and there was nothing to carry but the case. Thirteen years old. Violin under her arm in its student Gewa case. She sat on the arm of the chair Dr. Marsh sat in and opened the case on her lap and took out the chamois and wiped the rosin dust off the belly of the violin in small slow circles. On the left side of her neck, above the collar of her cardigan, a small pink callus had been forming for two months now where the chinrest lived. She was not aware of it, which was the point. She had cleared the bar so young that nobody had thought to put a bar there. She got grandfathered into freedom before she knew there was a cage.

"From the top," Jackie said.

They ran the Chopin étude first — Opus 10, No. 3, the one called "Tristesse," the one anyone's mother recognized — arranged for four pieces, Jackie's arrangement, the melody in the violin, the harmony voicings on the Baldwin, Max walking the root under Ace's brushes. Jackie had written out every chart in his own hand, the ink neat as a ledger. It came out of the four of them the way a good clock comes out of its case. Nothing missing.

Then "Somebody to Love" in A-flat major — the Mercury gospel piled up in stacked thirds, Elizabeth doubling the top line with the bow, Max and Ace holding the pocket. Then "Bohemian Rhapsody," the whole six-minute architecture, B-flat opening, the operatic middle stacked, the hard-rock vamp, the coda. The harmonies locked. Every chord where it went. The kind of rehearsal a band videotapes and sends to a label.

Dr. Marsh came down during the last verse.

He came down with the leather notebook under his left arm, the one he used for patients and lectures and his children. He did not sit right away. He walked across the carpet behind Jackie, behind Ace's kit, and stood at the Baldwin for a breath — and as the last chord rang Jackie, whose eyes were on the keyboard, did not see his father's right hand come out and settle, and did not see the thumb touch middle C. Not press. Touch. Half a beat. The key did not sound. The thumb came off. His father's hand closed, went to the spine of the notebook, steadied it. Then Dr. Marsh crossed to the chair by the wall and sat, and opened the notebook on his knee.

Jackie played the last resolving chord and lifted his hands.

"The Chopin was excellent," his father said. He was smiling the small careful smile. "Elizabeth, your intonation in the second phrase was exactly right."

Elizabeth said thank you and put the chamois back in its corner of the case.

Dr. Marsh stood. He walked to the Baldwin and rested his hand on Jackie's shoulder, the weight of it careful as a stethoscope.

"The Queen, Jackson. When you play it like that — controlled. Precise. Every note exactly where it belongs — " He paused. He was choosing his word. He found it. "You remind me of Glenn Gould. That kind of technical mastery. Mercury is a talent, but he is undisciplined. You've taken his chaos and made it civilized."

He squeezed the shoulder once. The notebook went back under his arm.

"Keep this up," he said, "and tomorrow will take care of itself."

The side stairs took him back up. The door at the top closed on its soft seal.

Civilized. Jackie sat with the word on him.

---

Ace packed first, because Ace always packed first, sticks into the stick bag, cymbals into the gig bag with a folded bath towel between them. Max coiled his cord over-under and slid the Precision into its case. Goodbyes at the side door. Feet going up the driveway in sneakers and a Chuck Taylor, a car door, a second car door, an engine, another engine. Quiet.

Elizabeth was still on the chair arm.

"You okay."

"Fine."

"Jack."

He looked at her. She had the chamois folded into its small square now and was closing the case in the way she closed books — not snapping the latch, pressing it shut.

"You know he stopped asking me to practice last year," she said. "I'd already done the job. He lets me alone." She looked at the Baldwin, not at him. "But you keep trying to make him hear something. And he doesn't hear music, Jack. He counts notes."

Jackie did not answer.

"Go to bed," she said. "Tomorrow's long."

She took the violin upstairs. The door at the top closed again.

---

He sat on the bench another minute with the fluorescent buzzing and the four little red Tascam LEDs glowing at the wall and the foam doing its patient work on every sound.

Then he played "Bohemian Rhapsody" for himself.

Not the arrangement. The record. He started at the operatic middle section where the voices stack, and he sang the *Galileo, Galileo, Galileo figaro* in his head because you could not sing it in a Marsh basement, and his left hand made the big jumping accompaniment that wasn't in any of the charts, and his right hand did the Mercury flourishes the charts had taken out, and for three minutes he was not an early-admission to The Juilliard School, 144 West 66th Street, New York. The ballast buzzed. The foam drank. The Tascam's LEDs held their small steady red.

Then the song ended.

Classical earned his father's approval. Rock earned his breath. He couldn't have both.

---

He gently lowered the piano lid. The soft wooden click went across the foam and was absorbed before it finished. He killed the basement lights at the switch by the stairs.

He went up.

He passed the study door, open a hand's width — his father at the desk inside, textbooks fanned out in the green pool of the banker's lamp, a pencil in his hand, checking one book against another for tomorrow's lecture. He passed the living room. His mother in the wing chair under the floor lamp, a novel on her lap, her eyes on the page and not on the page. He passed Elizabeth's door, closed, the thin line of her bedside light under it.

His own door closed behind him with the quiet click of a door hung right.

On the desk, the Juilliard envelope lay where it had lain for three weeks, cream laid paper, the letter knife slit along the top. Next to it, face down on the stack of old Curtis programs where he had put it in March, the small silver frame held the photograph he could not look at tonight.

He did not turn the photograph over.

He did not open the envelope again.

He took off his shoes, set them at the foot of the bed, and got under the covers in his clothes.

**END CHAPTER 22**

CHAPTER 25: EVE OF THE BATTLE

---

Dutton Road was quiet at a quarter to ten. Nick lay on top of his bedspread in his jeans and listened to the house tick the way houses did after everyone was supposed to be asleep. The refrigerator. A pipe in the wall. His mother's shoes coming off in the kitchen.

He got up.

The side door of the house opened onto the breezeway and the breezeway onto the garage, and in the garage the one bare bulb came on the way it always did — a half-flicker and then the yellow. The April 1975 Aerosmith calendar was still tacked over the bench where Dan had left it, the page turned to a month that would never get flipped again. The red Craftsman toolbox sat against the far wall, latches rusted shut. On the plywood lid, a Maxwell House can held a 9/16ths socket and a worn spark plug. Nick had not moved either thing in three years.

The $25 acoustic was on its stand by the door. He picked it up. He did not plug in. The Lincoln boys had gone home an hour ago — Stephen's Nova pulling away, Mark's laugh from the passenger window, David shouting something about tomorrow — and the garage still smelled of their sweat and his own, and of the motor oil that had soaked into the concrete long before any of them were born.

He sat on a milk crate in front of the toolbox.

He played "Dream On" in the dark, unplugged, the pick against the strings barely louder than the ticking house. He played it the way Dan had showed him one Sunday — thumb anchored, bend on the second fret, breathe on the pause. Halfway through the solo his left hand stopped where his father's hand had always stopped to nod, and he nodded at nobody, and he went on.

He finished. He set the guitar across his thighs.

He looked at the latches.

He did not open the toolbox.

After a while he turned off the bulb and sat in the dark with the guitar warming his legs, listening to a truck downshift on Route 20 a half-mile away, and he understood that tomorrow he would play for his mother and for the ghost in the toolbox and for the truck driver and for nobody, and that the order of those things was the only thing he still got to decide.

In the kitchen, his mother's light went out at ten-thirty.

---

Two miles north, on Maple Street, Dr. Richard Marsh's house faced a row of hedges clipped to the same height every April by the same man. Jackie's bedroom was on the third floor, under the eaves. The Steinway was two floors below him and might as well have been in another country.

He sat on the wide sill of the dormer window with his knees drawn up and the curtain half-drawn behind him. The streetlight on the corner laid a pale strip across the rug. His mother had gone to bed. His father was in his study, reading. The house was the kind of quiet that measured itself.

On the desk behind him, the Juilliard envelope sat on top of a stack of recital programs. Acceptance or waitlist, he hadn't opened it. He had promised himself he would not open it until after tomorrow, for reasons he had not examined.

Face down on the blotter, in a drugstore frame, was a Polaroid from Camp Elbanobscot, 1975 — three kids at the end of a dock, a borrowed guitar across one lap, a girl between the two boys laughing at something the photograph had not caught. He had turned it face-down in March. He had not turned it back.

Under his pillow, the little transistor radio was already on.

WBCN, 104.1, Boston, playing what WBCN played at a quarter to eleven on a Monday in May — some Dire Straits track, "Sultans of Swing," the guitar clean as a knife through paper. The DJ's voice came on at the end. It was not Maxanne's. Maxanne had been gone two years by then, though the station still sounded like a room she had walked out of.

He pressed his ear closer to the pillow. He had done this since he was eight, since he had first understood that the house had listening ears and that the radio was where people talked about music like it was a thing you loved, not a thing you graded.

The DJ announced the next song. Jackie did not catch the name.

He thumbed the dial. The radio clicked off.

Two floors below him, the Steinway sat closed in the dark, polished, waiting. He put his forehead against the window glass and watched the streetlight flicker once on Maple Street at ten-thirty.

---

On the other side of Sudbury, past the orchard and the cornfields and the long dip where Landham Road crossed the brook, the Lally farm sat low against the pines. The hogs had been fed and watered. The barn lights were off. A sow was grunting somewhere in the back pen, a soft complaint at nothing, the way sows did when they were settling.

Patty's bedroom was at the back of the house, over the mudroom. Wide pine floors. A braided rag rug her grandmother had made. A lamp with a yellowed shade that cast the room in the color of old paper. A *Rumours* poster was tacked to the slant of the wall — the black-and-white one, Stevie leaning on Mick — the corners curled from the woodstove heat that rose through the register in winter.

She lay on top of the quilt in her jeans and a white t-shirt, not sleeping.

On the little desk by the window, she had a sheet of her mother's stationery and a Bic pen. She had written *Dear Nick* and crossed it out, written *Dear Jackie* and crossed it out, written *Dear both of you* and crossed that out too. The sheet was in the wastebasket now, balled up the way she balled up things she meant.

A headlight — a late school bus from the Route 20 yard going home empty — swept across the ceiling on Landham Road and was gone.

Her transistor was on the nightstand, low. A DJ was reading a community bulletin. She was not really listening.

She caught herself humming. She had been doing it all night, the way some people chewed the inside of their cheek. *You can go your own way, go your own way* — the bridge, not the chorus. She got two bars in and the hum caught in her throat the way a splinter catches in a finger, and she put her hand to her neck and stopped.

She was not going to fix them. She had told herself that at St. Michael's and she told herself that now. She only wanted to stand on the stage tomorrow and sing a song she loved, and let them hear what that sounded like.

Out in the barn, the sow sighed and was quiet.

The lamp went out at ten-thirty.

---

The Lincoln-Sudbury parking lot lay empty under its one sodium lamp, the stage door locked, the gym dark. A freight train pulled east toward Boston along the Route 20 cut, and the night closed behind it.

**END CHAPTER 25**

CHAPTER 21: NICK'S REHEARSAL

The garage bay door stood up to the chest-high stop, lifted halfway for the air — May eighth in Sudbury, sixty-five degrees if it was a degree, the kind of spring night that felt warm only because April had set the bar so low. Crickets had started in the grass by the oil stain. Behind the Cavicchio fence a spring peeper was going in the wet low place, one note at a time, not fast. A Chevy with a bad belt whined down Dutton Road and faded toward the Horse Pond light.

Inside the garage the air was forty watts worse than outside. One bare bulb on a length of exposed Romex swung a finger's width when a kid walked under it. The Marshall practice amp on the milk crate was warm enough to put a palm on. The guitar case was open on the concrete, cables heaped in it like rope in a dinghy.

Nick stood in the middle of it with the twenty-five-dollar acoustic he'd walked out of a pawn shop in Framingham with the summer he was fourteen — four springs ago, Dan still around for one more year, the price Dan had paid because he'd said *don't tell your mother* and then told her at dinner that night himself. The guitar had a crack in the upper bout Nick had packed with wood glue the summer he was fifteen. His fingertips knew every raised grain on the neck.

Stephen Murphy had his Univox Hi-Flyer plugged into a little Kustom 2x12 borrowed off his cousin in Hudson. Univox was the cheap copy of the Mosrite the real players in Boston clubs used, and Stephen had saved for it out of a paper route and three-fifty an hour at the Sunoco on 126. It was the color of a Ford brake light. He'd tuned it four times already.

David Cassel sat on a crate behind a Ludwig four-piece his uncle had handed down, one cracked crash rivetted back together with a brass washer his father had drilled out on the basement bench. Mark Pianka had a Rhodes on loan from Mr. Wentworth — a Stage Piano out of the music-room closet that buzzed on the B below middle C if you leaned on it. Mark had figured out not to lean on it, mostly.

"One more time," Nick said.

"We've done it four times," David said.

"One more."

They ran "Dream On." Stephen's bass locked in under Mark's keyboard figure. David's snare hit was quieter tonight than it would be tomorrow — the neighbors closer at a milk crate's remove than they'd be at the back of an auditorium. Nick sang.

When they finished, Stephen laid the Univox flat on his thigh.

"Nick."

"Yeah."

"Whatever happens tomorrow. We're with you. Not because of your mom at Friendly's. You're the reason any of us started playing."

Mark was wiping Rhodes-sweat off the F key. "Freshman year you were the only one who didn't laugh when I came in with my grandmother's Casio. You said *can you play it.*"

David twirled a stick between his fingers and watched it. "You taught me the grip. Three lunches in a row, the music room."

"So tomorrow," Stephen said, "we play. Screw the rest."

Nick nodded once. He did not trust his voice yet.

"One more," he said, when he did. "Then go."

They ran it one more time. Then the Kustom cut and the Rhodes cut, and David laid the sticks crossed on the snare head the way a carpenter lays a level down, and they were packing up.

At the curb Stephen's father's '74 Nova sat idling with the headlights aimed at the garage. Mark's brother was five minutes out. David lived a quarter mile down Dutton and was walking. The three of them went out under the half-raised bay door with their cases and their cords, and at the end of the driveway Stephen said *Nick,* once, and Nick lifted two fingers off the neck of the acoustic, and Stephen got in the Nova and the Nova pulled away down Dutton and the headlights took the last of themselves with them.

The crickets came back up.

---

Grace stood on the back step in her Friendly's uniform with her hand on the storm-door handle and did not open it.

The laundry line ran from the porch post to the maple in the side yard and the line was empty — she had brought the sheets in at six the way she had brought them in every Thursday for twenty-three years. Across Dutton Road on the Connolly porch the orange cat sat on the railing with its tail hanging over the mailbox side. Up by the mill the Chevy with the bad belt passed again, coming back. The same one. The belt did the same thing.

From the open garage she could hear him finishing out. The kids were gone. It was just the one guitar now.

She was afraid of what he would do if he lost. She was afraid of what he would do if he won. Both fears were the same fear, and both fears had the same hand on the same chrome storm-door handle of the same house she had grown up in at twelve, in a different life, on a step she had been standing on when the first policeman came up the walk in October of '41 to tell her mother about her father. She did not open the door. She stood with her hand on the handle until the chrome warmed. Then she took her hand off and went in.

The storm door shut behind her on its own hinge.

---

In the garage Nick stood alone in the forty-watt yellow.

His left hand hurt. The pads of his fingers had gone past sting to something that was not quite numb. The high E bit him a little every time he landed on it, and he landed on it a lot, because "Dream On" started there and the bite got worse as the night went. His grip on the neck tightened and he made himself open the hand twice and close it.

He bent and picked up a pick off the concrete — Fender medium, the logo worn white down one side where his thumb had been. He turned it over. The other side still had the tortoise pattern readable. He set it on the Marshall next to the one already there and stood up.

The toolbox sat where it had sat for eighteen months, under the 1975 April calendar, red paint chipped at the corners, latch shut. On the Maxwell House lid beside it, the 9/16ths socket. Nick glanced at the latch once. Still shut. He did not go near it.

He sat on the milk crate. He put the acoustic across his lap. He worked his left hand open and shut twice, the way Dan had taught him to do when the tendon got tight — *shake it out, Nicky, don't fight it, shake it out —* and then he laid his fingers on the neck and played the piano intro to "Dream On" on six strings of gut and wire.

Don Kirshner had put a piano on the Aerosmith record in '73. Nick played the piano part on the twenty-five-dollar acoustic because there was no piano in the garage and because it was the only way he could play it alone. His right thumb picked the melody low on the neck. His left hand fretted slow. When he came to the bend at the end of the first phrase his fingertip bit and he breathed in through his nose and did not stop.

Outside, the crickets had gone quiet.

He did not notice at first. He was in the third phrase before he noticed. The peeper had stopped too. The Chevy with the belt was gone up the road. The night past the half-opened bay was holding still around what was coming out of the garage.

*You got the gift, Nicky.*

The Battle was eighteen hours away.

He played the passage through, alone, the acoustic bright and thin against the pegboard and the bare joists and the concrete, the way Dan had bent over him one Sunday afternoon in the summer he was fourteen and guided his hand on the neck until the fingering came right. When he stopped the crickets started back, first one, then two, then the whole yard, and the peeper came in behind the Cavicchio fence on its slow cadence, and the bare sixty-watt bulb on the Romex swung the width of a finger because a moth had hit it.

Nick set the guitar down in the case on the tangle of cables. He closed the lid. He did not latch it. He reached up and pulled the bay door down to the concrete with both hands, slow, the way Dan had taught him, easing the springs the last six inches so the counterweight did not slam.

On his way to the side door he did not look at the toolbox.

**END CHAPTER 21**

CHAPTER 24: PATTY RETURNS

May 14th, 1979. St. Michael's, Sudbury, a little after nine. The last car door in the parking lot had been Steve's Chevette — the hinge on the driver's side that whined if you opened it past halfway — and Patty had counted it the way she counted beats, and then she'd been alone.

She stayed in the pew. Rumours had packed up an hour ago. Kristy's amp had gone out first, then Robin's kick pedal, then Steve's snare in its padded bag, and then the three of them had hugged her at the parish-hall door the way you hug somebody the night before surgery — a little too long, a little too careful — and now the hall was just a hall again and the sanctuary was what it had always been on a Monday night, which was empty.

She had moved the guitar in here on purpose. The acoustic was a hand-me-down from her uncle in Hudson, a Yamaha FG-180 with a scratch along the lower bout where somebody at some wedding had set down a beer bottle and forgotten it. The finish had gone honey-amber the way old spruce did. It lived in a soft case with a broken zipper that she held shut with a shoelace.

She took it out. She sat it across her thigh. She tuned by ear because the pitch pipe was in her bag and the bag was two pews away and she could hear the low E against the silence in the nave without any help.

E. Flat. She bent the tuning key a hair. The string came up under her thumbnail with the small sweet creak of new bronze against bone nut. A. Fine. D. Fine. G. A hair sharp; she gave it back. B — B was always the one — she tuned it twice. High E. Fine.

She was wearing jeans with barn mud dried on the left knee, a flannel over the Rumours T-shirt she'd saved up for at Strawberries on Mass Ave, and her hair braided over her right shoulder. Her fingertips had the pad calluses guitar players get, little hard discs where the string bit in, and the back of her left hand had a pink line from last Tuesday — a strand of barbed wire that had caught her when she went in after a sow. On her right forearm, the half-circle bruise from a hoof step was going yellow at the edges. She smelled faintly of pig. She had known it getting into her truck and she had known it getting out of her truck and she was not going to apologize for it to a room full of saints.

She got up and walked to the rack of votives by the side altar. The red glass jars sat in three rows on a black iron frame, most of them unlit on a Monday. The box of long matches was on top. She took one, struck it against the strike strip, and the head caught with that small chemical pop. She held the flame to a wick in the second row. The wax made a tiny suck of air taking the fire, and then the flame straightened into an orange flower the size of her thumbnail, and the red glass around it went alive.

She did not say who it was for. She never said. She blew the match out and set it in the sand tray with the other spent ones and stood there for a second watching the flame jump inside the glass. Then she went back to the pew.

Above the main altar, behind the tabernacle, the big window was St. Michael with his foot on the dragon's neck and his sword down and through, the glass lead-seamed so that the dragon was the color of bottle-green and the saint was the color of a bruise healing. Incense from Sunday still hung in the wood. Melted wax. Worn oak. The Stations of the Cross marched around the nave in plaster relief, fourteen small reliefs she had known since she was seven. Jesus falls. Jesus falls again. Jesus falls the third time.

The hymnal was red. She had one in her lap from when Rumours had rehearsed here — Father Delaney let them use the parish hall if they didn't swear and if Robin wiped the floor under the kick drum — and she rolled it back and forth along her thigh while she thought, the pebbled leatherette cover making a soft dry sound on the denim.

She let her thumb open the camp notebook.

The letters were inside the back cover. Seven of them, folded small, paper gone soft at the creases the way paper did when you opened it too many times. Four from Nick. Three from Jackie. She took Nick's top one out and opened it across her knee. The handwriting was cramped and sideways-slanted like he was running out of room even though the page was half empty, and in the third line down he had crossed out *my dad* and written *my father* above it and then crossed that out too and put *him*. Three tries on two letters. The pen had pressed so hard on the last one that the paper had dimpled through to the back.

She folded it. She slid it back into the notebook.

Jackie's top letter was thinner paper, the kind with the faint blue lines. The handwriting went straight across the page like a prayer. Every *t* was crossed. Every *i* was dotted. At the bottom, where he'd written *I am learning the C-minor prelude and I can almost make it breathe*, he had underlined *almost* once, careful, with a ruler. Her thumb rode the crease. She put it back.

Nick's cramped urgent fingers. Jackie's ruler.

She thought about Jackie in the window booth at the café downtown last fall, lifting a sugar cube out of the bowl with the little silver tongs and setting it on the spoon and lowering it into the tea so he could watch it dissolve from underneath. He had done this whole operation while he was telling her that his father thought Queen was a phase. She thought about Nick at Friendly's in March, a tuna melt cooling in front of him because he was too busy drumming a tempo on the booth Formica with a butter knife to eat it, and the waitress calling him honey twice and him not hearing her either time.

She let the letters sit. She did not want to sort them anymore.

She pulled the guitar back onto her thigh and played a D. Then a G. She slid to a C and her ring finger missed the third fret and landed a buzz against the second, and she laughed — out loud, in the empty sanctuary, one small startled bark of a laugh — and St. Michael did not move and the dragon did not move and she played the C again and this time it rang.

Then, without meaning to, she was humming. It came up out of her the way weather came up out of a field. *Loving you / isn't the right thing to do.* She didn't sing the words. She hummed the line, just the shape of it, the small step-down at the end, her right hand picking a quiet D-flat bass note underneath it because the song wanted that bass note and her hand knew.

Camp Elbanobscot, the summer she was fourteen, the lake going copper at the end of the day. Nick's guitar had been out of tune and neither of them had cared. Jackie had played a chord nobody had asked for, a suspended thing with a fourth hanging in it, and her voice had come in over the top without thinking, and for about six seconds the three of them had landed inside one sound — lake water lapping the dock pilings, the sap-hot smell of pine, three voices and two guitars and nobody keeping count. They had not been trying. That was why it had worked. They had been breathing, and the breathing had happened to rhyme.

She hummed another bar. She was on the word the song wouldn't give her — the turn between *you* and *isn't* — when a car door went in the parking lot. Short, metal, far side.

Her thumb went still on the G string.

She listened. The car started. The car pulled out. It wasn't for her.

She put the hum back down and rested the guitar flat across her knees.

She reached into her bag and her fingers found the little transistor radio her brother had given her two Christmases ago. Panasonic, white, the antenna bent because it had ridden in too many glove compartments. She almost turned it on. WBCN would be on from last time; it was always on from last time. She took her hand out of the bag.

Not tonight.

She tuned the B string one more time because the B string was always the one. She played the opening of the song she wasn't going to play tomorrow — just the first four bars, for herself — and let it die against the stone. She put the guitar in the case. She tied the shoelace.

At the side altar the votive was still going. The red glass was warm when she passed a hand near it, not touching, just checking. She dipped two fingers in the holy-water stoup by the door and crossed herself the way her mother had taught her, quick, four points, sternum and shoulders, without closing her eyes.

She pushed the door open with her hip because the guitar case was in her right hand and the notebook was in her left. The night air came in smelling of cut grass and diesel from Route 20. Behind her, in the empty sanctuary, the little orange flower kept burning inside its red glass, and St. Michael kept his sword down through the dragon, and the hymnal sat on the pew where she'd left it with the print of her thumb on the cover.

She let the door close on its own soft seal.

**END CHAPTER 24**

CHAPTER 23: MAXANNE — THE EVE OF BATTLE

Three hours into the broadcast. One hour left.

The Heaven Hill paper cup has gone soft at the rim. I refill it. My hands on the console are steady now. Guilt doesn't shake you forever. It just sits down beside you and waits for the cue.

The ON AIR sign holds its red like an open wound. Behind the glass, the kid finally put the phone down. Quit scrolling about an hour ago. He's watching me the way you watch an old drunk at a bar who's about to say something true.

The Neve 8068 under my fingers was old when I left this station the first time. Faders worn smooth at the tips from a thousand hands. Coffee ring from '86 still there. Studio B still smells like the forty years of cigarette smoke nobody bothered to shampoo out of the walls, even after the state banned it in 2003. On the wall above the console, the old NAB cart rack — steel frame, thirty slots — is empty. Just the dust shadows where the brown-and-cream carts used to sit. Little gray rectangles. Ghosts of rotation.

The Pink Floyd LP is still cued on the turntable, needle up. Waiting. To my right, the demo cassette: *Demo — Nick/Jackie — un-Authorized — March 1979*. I picked it up an hour ago and I haven't put it down.

---

The Battle of the Bands was my idea.

I want that on the record before we go any further. Not Tom Andrews. Tom ran it. Tom executed. The seed was mine, planted in a pitch meeting in the fall of '76 — regional high school contest, WBCN sponsorship, a recording session for the winners. I sold it to management the way you sell anything to management: find the next Aerosmith before the next Aerosmith needs us. Drive the fifteen-to-twenty-fives. Attract the sponsors who wanted the kids.

Six months later, in April of '77, I left.

Elektra had offered me A&R. More money. More reach. I'd spent seven years in this building breaking bands — Aerosmith out of a dive in Allston, the Cars when every label thought Ric Ocasek was a weirdo with cheekbones. I told myself A&R was the next floor up. Same work, better budget. I was still going to find the next Neighborhoods. I'd just find them with a checkbook in my hand.

The Battle went off without me. Spring of '79. Tom called and asked if I'd sit the judges' panel. Elektra said yes before I did. Scout the room, sign somebody. The industry doesn't care which end of the microphone you hold. It only cares that you keep the line moving.

So I came back.

Not as WBCN. As Elektra. In a blazer I wouldn't have owned two years before.

---

May 15, 1979. Lincoln-Sudbury Regional High School auditorium. Nine hundred and eighty-five seats, every one of them filled, every one of them already decided. I sat on the judges' panel between two people whose names I have let myself forget, clipboard on my knees, pencil in my hand.

One concrete image I've kept for thirty years.

Nick Johnson's hands, before Nick played a note. Thumb flat-picking the low E to tune. Knuckles still raw from a week of rehearsal with no stopping. *Dan Johnson's hands*, I thought. *Nick has his father's hands.*

Across the stage, Jackie Marsh tuning too. Jackie's hands were clean. Long fingers. Surgeon's hands the way the father wanted them. The kind of hands that know what a metronome is.

They did not look at each other. Not during tune. Not during the set. Not once.

Grace was in the third row. Still in the polyester. Name tag *Grace* pinned on the apron she hadn't bothered to take off because she'd come straight from the shift. The seat next to her was empty. Dan should have been in it. Everybody in the room who knew pretended not to see the empty seat. I had never met Grace. Never have. I knew her from two rows up the way you know weather.

---

I didn't create their division.

Hop Brook did that. The cafeteria did that. Dan Johnson's crane cable in November of '77 did that. Dr. Marsh did that, at his kitchen table, in sentences about surgery and sensible futures. Class did that. America did that.

But I took a slow, private death and I put a ticket price on it. I saw two boys drifting and said, let's bring them back together onstage. For content. For sponsors. For a photograph in the Globe.

I didn't kill their friendship. But I gave class warfare a microphone. I sold tickets to watch innocence die. I turned tragedy into entertainment.

And then I called it opportunity.

---

Eleven forty-seven. Thirteen minutes.

Freddie Mercury's voice comes through the monitors from somewhere deeper than analog. He's been gone eighteen years. Thirty years of medicine too late.

I used to tell myself I left this station before I had to compromise. That leaving in '77 was the clean choice. A&R was just a different angle on the same work. I was still looking for the next Neighborhoods. I still had the ear.

Elektra was a cage with better carpet.

I signed the safe ones. I passed on the dangerous ones. I learned to say *demographic* with a straight face. I helped turn the kind of band I used to champion into the kind of band I used to warn kids about. The rebel DJ who wouldn't shut up became a woman in a blazer who filled out quarterlies and measured risk and told herself this was still music.

I went quiet. For thirty-two years.

The station brought me back tonight because nobody else wanted it. I drew short straw. Walked in at nine o'clock to play eulogy for my own life. On paper I'm the guest of honor. In the actual room I'm a mirror.

Four decades of rock radio. Forty-one years, give or take. The brochure says *fifty-six* because somebody in corporate couldn't count and nobody stopped them. Monday morning, 98.5 starts playing contemporary Christian out of this same transmitter. Jesus on the frequency we used to give Patti Smith. I don't know if that's irony or just America.

---

The demo cassette is warm in my palm. *un-Authorized.* Still unplayed. I haven't put it down since the ON AIR light came on.

The Pink Floyd LP waits. *Shine On You Crazy Diamond.* The memo says that's how WBCN goes out. Graceful. Elegiac. Ending by committee.

The clock gives me twelve minutes now.

Before I choose, there are two rooms you need to see. The night before the Battle. Dutton Road first — Nick's garage, his dead father's tools on the pegboard in the exact order Dan left them. Then across the brook, under the Marsh house, a finished basement made into a studio for a boy whose father is paying for the next fifteen years of his life in advance.

Two kids. Same hour. Four miles of road and one wooden bridge between them.

Neither of them knowing they'd already lost.

My hands are steady. The engineer behind the glass isn't blinking. I reach for the cart marked *Flashback — Marsh basement, May 14, 1979*, and I thumb the bourbon cup empty in one swallow, and I lean into the mic.

Stay with me.

**END CHAPTER 23**

I wrote the contest rules myself. Three months before the event, in my Elektra office with my name on the door, I drafted the tie-breaker clause. Small-print paragraph most panels never read. *In the event of equal scores, the panel may elect to declare co-winners.* I told myself I was being fair. I told myself I was hedging for quality.

## Timothy's Act III directives (verbatim in spirit)

1. **No feel-good ending. No sappy. No cliche.** The novel — and Nick, Jackie, and Maxanne — deserve better. Earn every beat with specific physical truth. If a sentence could appear in a USA TODAY puff piece or a YA teen-musician novel, cut it.
2. **Finish strong with Dickey / King / Lehane in the prose.** Dickey's body-in-the-woods attention; King's plain-spoken suburban physical dread; Lehane's Boston class weight and Catholic-guilt grammar. Walk This Way is a rock and roll novel. The rhythm must match — short sentences where the drum hits, long sentences where the solo runs.
3. **Dialogue must be real, honest, true.** Nick at 17 and 18 does not speak in paragraphs. He speaks in working-class New England fragments. Jackie at 17 and 18 speaks in precise clauses that crack under pressure. Maxanne in the booth at sixty-three speaks in broadcast rhythm, bourbon-cadenced, cigarette-paced. Nobody gives a speech. Every time a character is about to give a speech, pick the one true sentence inside it and let the rest go.
4. **The final song reversal (Ch 34) is the novel's climax.**
   - The corporate-approved final song is **"Shine On You Crazy Diamond" by Pink Floyd** (this is the real WBCN final song per `RESEARCH_INSIGHTS.md`; the prior draft's "Comfortably Numb" is wrong — fix it).

She is talking about Pink Floyd on air — what "Shine On" means, why it's a perfect elegy, why corporate picked it, why she almost plays it. **Her commentary on Pink Floyd must come first.** She needs to honor the choice before she refuses it.
   - Then — at the very last second, not four hours early — she says "fuck it" (or whatever terse equivalent the voice earns) and plays Nick and Jackie's demo instead.
   - WBCN goes dark at midnight. The real station did close at midnight (per Timothy). The demo must finish and the signal die right on the stroke.
5. **This novel honors Nick and reaches Jackie.** Nick (the real one) passed from ALS. Jackie (the real one) suffers severe depression and is housebound. If a sentence does not honor Nick or reach Jackie, cut it.
6. **"Make it count."** — in the words of the WBCN station manager.
