CHAPTER 34: THE LAST VOICE OF BOSTON ROCK — PART 2

Eleven-thirty. Half an hour left.

I've been talking for four hours. The battle. The tie. The 3 AM in Studio C. Dan's crane cable in '77. Grace in the third row in her Friendly's uniform. The tie-clause I wrote in an Elektra office a year before the boys ever knew my name. I have given WBCN the longest uninterrupted monologue in its fifty-six years and WBCN has not interrupted me, because WBCN is already gone. Only the signal is left, and the signal is waiting.

The phones have been ringing all night. I have let them ring. The board lights up in constellations, dies, lights up again. Somewhere down the hall a program director has given up and gone home to his wife. The kid through the glass — Kevin, Bruins hoodie, twenty-five, raised on Spotify — has put his phone down. He's watching me the way you watch a fire nobody lit on purpose.

Two objects on the console.

On the left, a cart. Brown plastic shell, cream label, Sharpie in somebody else's hand: SHINE ON YOU CRAZY DIAMOND — PINK FLOYD — FINAL TRACK — DO NOT REMOVE. Someone pulled it off the LP sleeve of *Wish You Were Here* this afternoon and loaded it into the NAB machine for me. Corporate's picked ending. Cued. Ready. All I have to do is punch it.

On the right, a seven-inch open-reel in a cardboard sleeve. Mike's handwriting, faded to the color of weak tea: *Nick/Jackie — un-Authorized — March 1979*. The sleeve is soft at the edges from thirty years of hands. The reel's been in my Cambridge study in a locked drawer the first of every month for three decades. I check it. I don't play it. I know what's on it. I carry the cassette of it in my purse the way a soldier carries a bullet that missed him — not as a souvenir, as proof.

The cassette sits on the console between the cart and the reel. Talisman. Witness. Unused tonight.

The ON AIR sign holds its red. Twenty-eight minutes until it doesn't.

WBCN signed on in 1968. I was twenty-four when I got here, in 1970. I'm sixty-three now. The subtraction is not simple.

---

I lean into the pop filter.

"I want to talk to you about Pink Floyd," I say. "Specifically about 'Shine On You Crazy Diamond,' which is on the cart machine in front of me, which somebody in corporate in North Carolina decided three weeks ago was how this station should end. I want to tell you why they're right."

The phones go off again. I don't look.

"The song is from *Wish You Were Here*. 1975. David Gilmour wrote the opening four-note guitar phrase — G, A-flat, E, B — and when Roger Waters heard it he stopped what he was doing and said this is him. He meant Syd Barrett. Syd was Pink Floyd's founder. The original frontman. The lyricist. The one who named the band — took two old Carolina bluesmen, Pink Anderson and Floyd Council, and made them one word. Everything Pink Floyd became was built on top of Syd Barrett, and by the time they sat down to make *Wish You Were Here* Syd was already gone. Not dead. Gone. Acid, mostly. A head that couldn't come back from where he'd taken it. He was twenty-four."

I pick up the cart. Weigh it in my palm. The plastic is warm from the lamp.

"They recorded the record and one afternoon a fat bald man in a raincoat wandered into the control room at Abbey Road, and for ten minutes the band didn't recognize him. It was Syd. He'd walked over. He listened to the song they'd written about him and he smiled politely and he went home and he never played guitar again in public for the rest of his life. He died in 2006. Three years ago, July. He was sixty."

My voice is bourbon-low. Heaven Hill paper cup on the console, gone soft at the rim.

"'Shine On You Crazy Diamond' is about burning so bright at the beginning that the rest of your life is a long dim afterward. It's about the one who couldn't make the compromise and didn't survive not making it. It's about a band that built a cathedral on the bones of a friend they couldn't save. It's a nine-part suite. It opens a record and it closes a record. You can't put it on in the car. You have to sit down for it."

Kevin through the glass has his hand on the fader. Waiting for my cue.

"Corporate picked this song because it sounds like grief without committing to any. Because it's long enough to run out the clock. Because the Christian broadcasting people taking this frequency at one minute past midnight needed something that would end the old story quietly so the new story could begin. And I will say this, because I have to say it on the air before I do anything else tonight — corporate got it right. Accidentally. For the first time in thirty years of corporate getting everything wrong, somebody in North Carolina picked the correct song for a rock station going dark. Syd Barrett deserves it. Pink Floyd deserves it. The people who spent fifty-six years listening to this frequency deserve it. 'Shine On' is the elegy. I mean that. I'm ready to play it."

I am. I mean it all the way down to the hand on the cart.

The VU meters idle. The reel to my right waits in its sleeve. The ON AIR holds red.

---

And then — nothing dramatic, just a small thing in the chest — I look at the reel.

Syd Barrett has Pink Floyd. Syd Barrett has a cathedral and a nine-part suite and a record that sold six million copies and a fat bald afternoon at Abbey Road that's been told so many times it's its own myth. Syd Barrett is fine. Syd Barrett does not need my airtime.

Nick Johnson has four minutes and forty-three seconds in a drawer in my house.

"Sorry, Syd," I say into the mic.

I set the cart down. I pick up the reel.

My hands know this motion. They've known it since I was twenty-four. The reel fits the spindle like a key in a lock that was cut for it. I thread the tape across the capstan, past the heads, onto the take-up. The leader is the color of old butter.

---

"Okay," I say. "New plan. I'll get in trouble for this. It doesn't matter who with.

"May 15, 1979. Lincoln-Sudbury Regional High School auditorium. Battle of the Bands, WBCN-sponsored, nine hundred and eighty-five seats, every seat full. Two bands. The Crown Jewels — a kid named Jackie Marsh on a Casio with a cracked middle C, and three others. The Aerosmith-Led Zeppelin tribute band — a kid named Nick Johnson on a hand-me-down Stratocaster, and three others. These two boys had grown up on the same brook, played on the same mini-bike trails, traded baseball cards in the same middle school cafeteria, and by the spring of '79 they weren't speaking. The town had done its work. Class did its work. A crane cable in November of '77 did its work. They tied. I made sure they could. I wrote the tie-breaker clause in October of '78 in an office in New York with my name on the door and I left the trap baited for a year before the trap closed.

"They played that tie for the room. Then at 2 AM Grace Johnson drove her son, and somebody's mother or father drove Jackie, to this building. I'd pulled a session engineer out of bed. Studio C. Two microphones four feet apart. No amp. Nick through a DI box, Jackie on a Yamaha upright. One take. No overdubs. 'Sweet Emotion' folded into 'Bohemian Rhapsody,' Aerosmith bleeding into Queen, a bar of 'Walk This Way' strutting through the middle just to see if it could. Four minutes and forty-three seconds. A stumble at the twelfth fret that Jackie caught on a crushed piano note and turned into the best sound in the recording.

"Then they shook hands in the hallway and went home to the people who'd already chosen them. Nick to the Army. Jackie to Juilliard. Me back to the label. I put the reel in a drawer. I've checked it the first of every month since Reagan. I have never played it. I am going to play it now. For you. Full volume. The way I used to, before I learned to ask permission."

The kid behind the glass has taken his hand off the fader. Something has happened to his face I will think about later.

"This is how rock was supposed to crash the silence," I say. "One time only. Stay with me."

I press play.

---

The VU meters slam red. My signature. The engineers used to hate it. The listeners never did.

D minor. Jackie's Yamaha. The chord fills the booth, fills the building, fills 104.1 FM from the Cape to the New Hampshire border — fifty thousand watts, for the last time tonight. The chord hangs in the air like a held breath the room has been waiting for since 1968.

Then Nick's guitar enters. Sweet Emotion stripped down to its bones. Clean, exposed, a boy playing at 2 AM in a room where anger did not help and he'd finally found that out. I've heard this tape two hundred and forty times in my head. I have never heard it out loud. The speakers give it dimensions my memory couldn't — the hum of the Studio C walls, the breath before a phrase, the slight hiss of Mylar wound on a plastic spool that cost forty cents wholesale in '79.

The two songs find each other. Jackie's left hand doubles Nick's riff an octave high, then lets go, and the Queen melody rises up out of the piano the way a river carries a leaf. The stumble at the twelfth fret. The crushed note. The crack that lets the light in. The hard rock section — both of them digging in, thirty seconds of controlled fury, the kind of fury that is actually tenderness with nowhere else to go. Two beats of silence.

The final chord. D minor. Sustain pedal down. The note rings and rings and fades.

Four minutes and forty-three seconds. The reel turns on into leader. I stop the machine. The spindle clicks.

The booth is quiet in a way no booth has ever been quiet in this building.

---

I lean into the mic one more time.

"This is Maxanne Sartori, signing off."

A beat. The clock on the wall reads 11:59.

"The music was real. Goodnight, Boston."

The ON AIR sign dies at midnight. Not a second off. Fifty-six years of red light and then no red light. The booth drops to emergency fluorescent, the color of old newsprint, and the absence of the red is louder than anything I ever played through this microphone.

Transmitter silence. Not quiet. Empty. The space where something used to be.

Twelve-oh-one. Static, then smooth. A man's voice mixed too hot, processed through reverb, the audio equivalent of a smile with nothing behind it.

*You're listening to JOY FM, bringing you the good news in music and ministry.*

A synthesizer choir fills the booth where Studio B used to live. I laugh once, sharp, half a sob, and the acoustic foam eats it.

---

Kevin opens the booth door. He stands in it. He does not speak. I understand we are not going to speak.

I leave the reel on the playback machine. Someone from JOY FM can inherit it with the rest of the ghosts. I pick up the cassette off the console and put it back in my purse where it has lived. I leave the Pink Floyd cart where it sits, honor guard for a suite that did not get its airtime.

The hallway's moving boxes have not moved. The lobby is darker than when I came in. Outside, August in Boston, asphalt and harbor, the antenna tower dark against the sky for the first time in fifty-six years.

My Volvo wagon is the only car in the lot. Twelve years old. I get in and close the door and the silence wraps around me the way Hop Brook wraps around a stone.

My phone buzzes.

A text from Sophie. My niece. Nineteen. Emerson. Thinks radio is what old people did before podcasts.

*Aunt Max did you play that song?? Someone recorded it someone put it on YouTube.*

A second text, already landing.

*It is BLOWING UP.*

I open the laptop on the passenger seat. The WBCN WiFi still works because nobody's thought to kill it yet. YouTube loads in the blue glow.

TWO GUYS WHO SHOULD HAVE BEEN FAMOUS — WBCN FINAL BROADCAST. Posted fourteen minutes ago by BostonRockRIP. Thumbnail of the antenna tower in Impact font.

50,000 views.

I refresh. 78,000.

The comments scroll past the way the request line used to scroll at eleven on a Friday night.

*1979??? This sounds like it could be today.*

*Who are these kids and how do I find them.*

*Sitting in my car in the parking lot of a CVS in Quincy crying.*

*Aerosmith plus Queen = this. How is this not a record.*

*Whoever played this on her last broadcast is a legend.*

*The Neighborhoods opened for the Cars at the Rat in '79 and these guys never even made the card. This is criminal.*

*RIP WBCN. Thank you Maxanne.*

I refresh. 140,000. 212,000. Twelve-thirty, three hundred thousand. The number climbs like something alive.

My phone rings. 212. New York. I don't answer. It rings again. 617. I don't answer. 310. Los Angeles. The calls stack up the way planes stack over Logan in weather. A voicemail from a producer at NPR. A voicemail from a writer at Pitchfork. A text from Carter Alan: *Maxanne what did you do.* A text from a number I don't know: *do you know where they are.*

One million views at 1:14 AM.

The signal has left the building. The signal has left me. The signal has gone out onto the night like water finding a crack it has been waiting three decades to find.

I am crying. Not sadness, not happiness. Some older thing my face knew before I did.

I close the laptop. The car goes black. I sit there in the Volvo in the empty lot with my hands on the wheel and I let myself think what I have not let myself think for thirty years.

Somewhere in a practice room on Mass Ave, on a Wednesday afternoon a month from now, a man in his late forties will be sitting at a Steinway Model B teaching an undergraduate about voice leading. Someone will come to the door with a laptop. Somebody will say, you have to hear this. He will not move at first. He will listen all the way through, four minutes and forty-three seconds, with his hands in his lap and his eyes closed. And when it ends he will lift his hands and put them on the keys, and he will play the D minor chord, just the chord, just once — and he will nod, very slightly, the way people nod when they finally hear somebody say out loud the thing they had decided they were alone with.

That's enough. That's what the tape is for. That's what the frequency was for, all along.

The reel turns, somewhere, in some kid's bedroom in Quincy, in some apartment in Somerville, in some dorm in Ann Arbor, in some kitchen in Manchester, New Hampshire, at one-twenty in the morning on August twelfth, two thousand and nine. Two boys in a room that no longer exists are still playing. The harmony found its receivers.

I turn the key. The Volvo catches on the second try. I drive out onto the Pike heading west, toward Cambridge, toward home, and I leave the radio off.

**END CHAPTER 34**

# Walk This Way — Draft 3.2 Canon Addendum

This document supplements `_SUBAGENT_BRIEF.md`, `_ACT3_BRIEF.md`, `DECISIONS_LOCKED.md`, and `RESEARCH_INSIGHTS.md`. It captures new canon established after the author's review of the Act I/II/III Scalpel & Hose passes. **All Draft 3.2 subagents read this before any chapter work.**

Everything in the prior briefs still holds unless explicitly superseded here.

---

## Directive from the author (paraphrased)

> Keep the story real and honest and gritty and determined. Keep *The Loss of Innocence* at the center of this small Boston-suburb town. The novel is the reveal of *The Best Band That Never Was* — Nick, Jackie, and the Lincoln Boys, if they had stayed together.
>
> Chapter titles (pre-1980 rock songs) are a final-pass decoration. **Do not let chapter-title songs influence the writing.** Write the chapters first. Rename later.

---

## Canon change 1 — Dr. Marsh is a pianist, not a guitarist

The prior draft established Dr. Richard Marsh as a man who had given up the guitar for his academic career, a mirror of Dan Johnson (who played guitar secretly in the garage). The author has corrected this: Dr. Marsh is a **former classical pianist** who abandoned performance for psychology. The mirror is sharper this way — Dan hid his guitar in the garage; Dr. Marsh closed the piano lid and walked away — *same regret, different instrument, opposite class expression.*

Consequences:

- Jackie learning piano is his father's abandoned instrument inherited as a projected dream.
- Nick learning guitar is his father's alive gift passed hand to hand.
- Jackie and Nick share *music in their bones* across different instruments. The mirror is at the level of parental sacrifice, not instrument.
- The existing "Dr. Marsh's hand on the Baldwin's middle C" (Ch 22) and "his hand on the Yamaha fallboard backstage" (Ch 26) are PERFECT for a pianist and need no change.
- The existing "Dr. Marsh's fingers closing a chord shape on the wine-glass stem" (Ch 17) can stay — a pianist forms chord shapes too; the three-finger triad reads equally as piano.
- The existing "Dr. Marsh glancing at Nick's callus pattern" (Ch 14) must be reframed. A pianist would NOT know a guitarist's specific fretting callus. But he would recognize a musician's hands — the unconscious committed posture, the callus at all, the small ghost of a wound-G scar. The crack becomes: he sees a kid committed to an instrument and looks away because his own commitment is buried. Still a crack. Not intimate-same-instrument recognition; committed-musician recognition.
- The existing "phantom twelfth fret" pinky flex (Ch 30) must change. A pianist doesn't reach for a fret. Change to a phantom-piano reach — the pinky uncurling once for a low octave his thumb hasn't touched in thirty years, or similar.
- The "gave up the guitar" references in Ch 32 (Jackie's bankbook monologue) become "gave up the piano." Associated verbs change — a piano isn't packed in a case and put in an attic; it was abandoned, the lid closed, the sheet music boxed.

This retcon is being applied to Draft 3.1 **before** Wave 1 begins.

---

## Canon change 2 — Grace's father, the scandal, the suicide

New backstory (subtle, not heavy-handed — the author's directive holds):

- **Arthur Halloran** (Grace's father — placeholder name; author may rename). Sudbury-based financier / broker. Big house on Dutton Road. "The wealthy influential guy in town."
- **Fall 1953:** Halloran is caught in a **Boston-area securities scandal** (broker fraud, commingling client funds, possibly a land-deal Ponzi — the precise legal mechanism is deliberately vague; fraud of the era). Federal indictment lands. Twenty-two-month sentence looming.
- **Late 1953 (late fall):** Halloran commits suicide at home to avoid prison and disgrace. Sudbury gossip is immediate and unkind.
- **Grace is 16, a junior at Lincoln-Sudbury in the class of 1955.** She witnesses the full collapse: the big house sold, the family moved into a rented duplex near Route 20, her social standing dropped from Ramper-tier to Reg overnight. Friends she'd known since first grade treat her differently. Some stay loyal. Most don't.
- Grace finishes her junior and senior years in the working-class geography of the town. This is where she first sees Friendly's from the *behind the counter* side of the class line — though she doesn't start working there until '56.
- **1955:** Graduates L-S.
- **1956:** Marries Dan Johnson (ironworker, working-class, steady, quiet). Takes the Friendly's waitress job at 19. Dan and Grace settle in.
- **1956–~1975:** Halloran's widow (Grace's mother) dies sometime in the late 1960s of stroke or illness — the family home has by now been sold, repurchased, or remained in a sibling's hands; the author can dramatize or leave implicit.
- **By 1977:** Dan and Grace are established Sudbury working-class. They have reclaimed (or rented, or inherited) the old Halloran house on Dutton Road. Per Ch 12 canon: "*this had been her parents' house and the world had been a different shape.*" This is now load-bearing — the house she lives in is her childhood home, the place where her father died.

### Author directive on Grace

> Grace and Dan are that Sudbury couple that never leaves town. They grew up in Sudbury and never left. Many real Sudbury lifers fit this description.
> The backstory should mostly NOT be shown. It's context. The reader feels it in Grace, doesn't learn it in a flashback.

Rendering rules:

- **No flashback scene** to 1953. Not a single sentence of direct dramatization.
- **Subtle surface hints only.** The chrome-handle flash in Ch 19 (existing) is perfect. The library-varnish-she-knew-as-a-girl in Ch 18 (existing) is perfect. The banister worn thin *under her father's hand and her own* in Ch 18 (existing) is perfect. Wave 2 may deepen these by exactly ONE concrete image — a framed family photograph that isn't on a wall anymore, a particular recipe card from her mother in a kitchen drawer, a specific wedding-china plate. One image. No paragraph. No exposition.
- Grace does **not** speak about her father. Not to Nick, not to Mary Murphy, not to anyone. His name may appear once in the full novel, or not at all.
- Dan knew the story but didn't press. He married her after, not before, knowing.
- One consequence the text can show: Grace's wariness around wealth. She never covets it. She's been on both sides.

### Fix required in Ch 21 rewrite

The Ch 21 rewrite currently contains the line:

> "the same chrome storm-door handle of the same house she had grown up in at twelve, in a different life, on a step she had been standing on when the first policeman came up the walk in October of '41 to tell her mother about her father."

This is wrong. Grace was four in October 1941 and her father's death was in 1953. **Fix to:**

> "the same chrome storm-door handle of the same house she had grown up in, the same step she had been standing on when the two men from the District Attorney's office came up the walk in the late fall of '53 to ask her mother if she knew where her father kept his papers."

(Or similar — keep the rhythm but correct the date and the specific authority. "Policeman" becomes "men from the DA's office" because it's financial crime, not ordinary crime. If the author prefers "policeman," use one patrol officer accompanying the DA men.)

---

## Canon change 3 — Jackie 2009: pre-depressive decline

Per the author, Jackie in 2009 is:

- Divorced.
- No kids.
- Teaching music theory at Berklee.
- **Unhappy.** Beginning the slow decline into full depression. Not yet housebound. Not yet broken. But the first internal coordinates of the disease are taking root.

Rendering rules:

- The man at the Berklee Steinway (Ch 34 closing imagination) must carry this. When he listens to the tape and plays the D minor chord, he is not a contented academic having a wistful moment. He is a man who has been alone with the wrong version of himself long enough that solitude has become architecture. The chord is not nostalgia; it is a small outward signal that the frequency still reaches him — that he has not gone entirely silent yet.
- Ch 33 Section II (Jackie / Manhattan August 1979) can be retrofitted in Wave 2 with one concrete physical beat that foreshadows this: a moment in the practice room when Debussy is done and Jackie sits still for longer than he should, not practicing, not resting, the piano warm under his hands and his hands not moving.
- **No diagnosis.** No word "depression." No clinical framing. Physical truth only.

This is the part of the book that is *for the real Jackie* — housebound in 2026, depression as his daily weather. The last image must say *you are seen* without saying it.

---

## Canon change 4 — Friendly's as ironic quadrant melting-pot

Per the author:

- Friendly's on Route 20 is where all four quadrants of Sudbury brush shoulders. The other genuine cross-quadrant space is The Dump on Saturday mornings. Friendly's is The Dump with ice cream.
- The irony of the name ("Friendly's") is the recurring Lehane-note: the town is not always friendly, especially not across quadrant lines. But Friendly's is literally the one restaurant where the Rampers' dad, the Rollers' dad, the Rats' older sister home from college, and the Regs' mom all eat at the counter at the same time on a Saturday.
- Grace working the Friendly's counter for 23 years means she has poured coffee for every adult in Sudbury at least once. She knows everyone's order. Everyone knows her name. None of them know her family story.

CHAPTER 11A

April in Sudbury was all mud. Hop Brook ran brown under the Route 117 bridge, loud enough to hear from the Lincoln-Sudbury front walk, and the lawn in front of the school had gone to that late-mud color that wasn't green yet and wasn't dirt anymore — the color of a boot print that had filled with water and frozen and thawed a dozen times since March. The parking lot was a lattice of tire ruts. A kid coming up the walk stepped wrong and went in past the ankle of his sneaker, said a word his mother wouldn't like, pulled his foot out with a sucking sound, and kept walking. Nobody looked. April.

It was seven-forty-five in the morning, and the buses were unloading in a slow brake-squeal procession at the circle. The first bell would go in four minutes.

Carl Marquis's '66 Impala came in off Lincoln Road from the south, throwing gravel, the muffler louder than it had been yesterday and louder tomorrow than it was today. Nick was in the passenger seat. He had his book bag between his feet and a quarter-eaten Hostess donut in his hand and his hair still wet at the back from the shower he'd taken at six-thirty because Grace had run the hot water down while doing dishes before Friendly's. The radio was on an AM station playing something that was neither good nor bad — just noise to fill the seven miles from Marquis's driveway to the school lot. The speaker in the driver's door buzzed on the high notes. It had buzzed since Carl and his father put the dash back together in November, and Carl had looked at it twice and decided it was a winter project, and then it had become a spring project, and now it was just the sound the car made.

Nick got out. He slammed the door the way you slam the door of a car like that — a second slam, because the first one never catches. Carl was already loping around the front, bag over his shoulder, hair in his eyes.

Up the walk, twenty yards away, a wood-paneled Buick Estate wagon pulled up to the curb. The wagon was clean. The wagon was always clean. Dr. Richard Marsh had Saturday-morning habits about wax and a chamois, and it showed. Jackie got out of the passenger side, closed the door with the small respectful click a kid closes a clean car with, and lifted his hand once to the driver's-side window without looking at his father's face. The Buick pulled away. Jackie stood on the curb a beat longer than he had to, adjusting the strap of his book bag, and then he moved up the walk toward the front doors.

His loafers were polished. The bottoms of his jeans were an inch dark with Dutton Road mud because he had walked across the lawn yesterday to save thirty seconds and that mud did not come out without a brush and Lava soap and Jackie had not had the time. He noticed it on the walk now, the small pull of dried mud against the denim at every step.

Nick was fifteen yards to his left, coming in from the parking lot at a diagonal. Nick saw him. His eyes went to Jackie the way a dog's head turns when another dog walks by — before the thinking gets there. Then Nick looked down at his own boots, at the donut in his hand, at the cigarette butt somebody had ground out in the gravel by his toe, and kept walking. Jackie's line and Nick's line converged toward the same set of double doors and stopped converging about eight feet before the doors, because Jackie moved toward the right-hand door and Nick moved toward the left, and they passed through at the same moment through doors hinged at different walls, and neither one looked at the other, and then they were inside and the hallway noise took them and they went in separate directions without a sentence between them.

The bell rang. In the window of the front office, a secretary picked up a rotary phone and began to dial.

Third period. Bay three.

The auto shop sat at the far end of the east wing in a building that had started its life as an agricultural annex and still looked it — cinderblock walls painted the color of instant mashed potatoes, corrugated steel doors that rolled up on greasy chains, and a concrete floor that sloped a half-inch toward a drain at the back that Mr. Harrington had been meaning to rod out for six years. Bay one was the classroom side, chairs in rows facing a chalkboard where Harrington sketched carburetor diagrams with a piece of white chalk held like a cigarette. Bays two and three were alive. Bay two had a '68 Impala up on jack stands, the hood yawning open, the radiator pulled. Bay three had Nick's project and Carl's project — a small-block Chevy 327 on an engine stand, stripped, the heads off, the valve train laid out on a piece of cardboard on the workbench in the order they came out.

The shop smelled like Brakleen and hot metal and shop hand-soap, the gritty orange kind in the gallon pump by the wash sink. Somebody's transistor radio sat on the bench by the compressor, tuned to WBCN, the volume low enough that Harrington wouldn't make them shut it off. Charles Laquidara's morning show was long over — Big Mattress ended at ten. It was a woman's voice now on the air, for the last days it would be, though the boys in bay three didn't know that and wouldn't have made anything of it if they did. The signal rode the fluorescent hum in the high frequencies the way a cicada rides a summer.

Nick had a socket wrench and a head bolt that had decided it didn't want to come. He leaned into it. His wrists were oil-dark to the cuffs, and there was a smear of black grease on his cheekbone from where he had scratched a mosquito bite an hour ago without thinking about his hands first. Carl was across the engine stand, a torque spec sheet in one hand and a cup of shop coffee in the other. The coffee was bad. Everybody said the coffee was bad. Everybody drank it.

"Break or lean on it," Carl said.

"I'm leaning on it."

"Lean harder. It's a bolt, not your grandmother."

Nick leaned. The bolt went a quarter turn and then another and then it broke free and came out in his hand clean, and he set it on the cardboard in its place in the line, and Carl made a small approving sound and went back to the torque sheet.

The door from the corridor opened and Donnie Rossi's cousin came through. His name was Anthony — Ant, to everyone — and he was a junior, and he was not supposed to be in the shop during third period because he had study hall in the cafeteria. He had a folded green hall pass in his fingers and a face that said he had no intention of explaining himself to Harrington because Harrington had stopped asking two years ago. Ant came up the aisle between bays two and three with his hands in the pockets of a Raytheon-blue work jacket that had been his uncle's before it was his, and he stopped at Nick and Carl's engine stand and looked down at the heads on the bench.

"You doing the valves today?"

"Reseating," Carl said.

"Harrington letting you grind em?"

"He said he'd do it. He's not doing it. So it's gonna be me doing it and him telling me I did it wrong."

Ant laughed. It was a good laugh — short, no teeth, the laugh of a kid who had been the youngest in a loud house and had learned to fit his amusement into other people's sentences.

Ant was a Roller in every sense Harrington would have recognized. He owned, in partnership with his brother Frankie, a 1970 Nova that lived in the driveway of a split-level on Route 20 behind the sheet-metal shop where his father was foreman. The Nova had a rebuilt 350 in it and rust through the back quarter panels and a bench seat his mother had reupholstered herself in brown vinyl from a roll she'd found at a yard sale in Marlborough. Ant knew a carburetor the way a piano kid knows a scale. His hands had the same thing Nick's had. He was going to work at his uncle's garage on Boston Post Road when he graduated, and everybody in his family already knew it, and Ant was fine with it — Ant had been fine with it since he was twelve.

"Friday night," Ant said, leaned on the bench. "We going or we not going?"

"Going where."

"Kevin said the trails. His brother's got that Yamaha. We're gonna ride til dark and then go to Store 24."

"I can't. I told my mother I'd get home by nine."

"Why you gotta be home by nine."

"Cause I told her I would."

Ant looked at Carl. Carl shrugged one shoulder.

"You heard about Gary," Ant said.

"Gary who."

"Gary Hagan. Broke his collarbone on the trails last weekend. Went over the handlebars on the big hill behind the transformer. He's in one of those sling things, his arm strapped to his body. His mother made him sit in the kitchen and told him he wasn't going to play JV baseball this spring, and he cried. A sixteen-year-old kid, crying at the kitchen table over JV baseball."

"Jesus," Nick said.

"Yeah. Jesus. So — Friday night. Trails. But carefully."

"Carefully," Carl said, and made the word sound like the opposite of itself.

Harrington came out from his office at the end of bay one. His coveralls were oil-black at the knees and pockets the way they had been for thirty years, and he had a cigarette tucked behind his ear he wasn't going to smoke until lunch. He gave Ant a look that was not a question so much as a timer. Ant pushed off the bench, folded the hall pass a little tighter, and started down the aisle.

"Nine o'clock," Ant called back.

"Nine o'clock," Nick said, and did not look up from the head bolts.

When the door closed, Carl tilted his head toward the engine. "Your mother's gonna let you out at nine."

"My mother's working the four-to-close at Friendly's. I'm letting myself out at nine."

Carl grinned. The grin stayed on the torque sheet and didn't find Nick's face. "She ever ask who she's leaving home."

"Not lately."

The radiator clanked in the corner, the one-pipe steam kind, and the '66 Chevelle hood leaning against the wall next to it gave back the clank as a faint metal shiver. The Chevelle was somebody else's project, somebody nobody had seen in three weeks. Primer grey. A pencil mark on the fender where the paint guy had measured for the body line. Nick looked at it and looked away. In his peripheral vision, the wall clock clicked up another minute, and the radio woman said something about Aerosmith on a record that was coming out in the fall, and the shop went back to its own sound.

Glass Corridor. Fourth period. Lunch A.

Lenny Henderson was sixteen and had been smoking for fourteen months, which meant he was still in the phase where he was proud of it and not yet in the phase where he was tired of it. He was sitting on the floor of the Glass Corridor with his back against the brick dado wall, his legs out straight in front of him, a paperback copy of *The Stranger* open on his thigh. The paperback had no cover. The cover had come off on the T on a Saturday back in February when he'd stuffed the book in his jacket pocket with a roll of dimes and sat on it for forty minutes, and now the book was just pages and a bent spine, which he preferred.

The Corridor ran twenty yards between the cafeteria and the arts wing, all dirty glass on the south side and brick on the north, and the two o'clock April sun came through the glass at an angle that turned the cigarette smoke into a physical thing — a column of soft yellow light standing in the middle of the hallway, slowly swirling, with the ash motes moving through it the way plankton moves through a shaft of undersea sun. An ashtray on a metal stand sat at the cafeteria end, chrome top, overfilled. Friday. The custodian would empty it Monday.

Lenny was rolling a cigarette one-handed because he could. He had learned to do it from a junior named Phil Koslowski who had learned to do it from his older brother who had been in the Navy. Lenny's left hand was holding the book open. His right hand had the paper between the first two knuckles of his index and middle fingers, the Top tobacco tin balanced on his thigh, and he was shaking tobacco into the paper with a tilt of the tin that was almost elegant. He rolled. He licked. He sealed. He tucked the cigarette behind his ear next to a pencil.

Two stools down — well, two brick-dado sections down; the Corridor had no stools — Maggie Doherty was sitting with her knees up and her head against the glass. Her jacket was leather and cracked at the elbows and she had bought it from a cousin in Dorchester last summer for twenty dollars. She was writing something in a composition book with a ballpoint pen that kept skipping. Farther down, a junior named Walt was reading a paperback Dostoevsky that was in worse shape than Lenny's Camus. The three of them weren't talking. The Corridor at lunch was not a place where people talked much. The point of the Corridor was that you could be with other people without having to perform being with other people. The smoke did the work.

A chemistry teacher came through from the cafeteria end, carrying a stack of lab reports, on her way to the arts wing for reasons none of the kids could imagine and didn't try to. She walked past the ashtray, past Lenny, past Maggie, past Walt, without turning her head. Her heels made the small solid sound heels made on waxed linoleum. She was gone through the far door in seven seconds. The ashes from her passing shifted in the yellow sunlight and resettled. Lenny took the cigarette from behind his ear and lit it with a Zippo that had been his grandfather's and that he had come to possess through a conversation with his mother he would never tell anyone about. He drew, held, let it out toward the glass. The glass fogged a square of itself and cleared.

Lenny Henderson lived on Maple Street in a five-bedroom colonial with a flagstone walk and a tennis court behind the garage. His father was a dermatologist with an office in Newton and a second house on the Cape. Lenny's mother had a standing appointment at Lord & Taylor on the second Thursday of every month. The tennis court had been resurfaced in October. Lenny had not played on it. Lenny had not played on it since he was eleven, when he had gone one day without being told to and had beaten his father in three sets, and his father had smiled and hugged him and then never asked him to play again.

Nobody in the Corridor knew any of this. Maggie had been to Lenny's house exactly once, the previous October, on a Friday when the family was in Chatham, and Lenny had taken her through the kitchen and out the back slider to the court and they had stood on the baseline in the dark with their hands in their pockets and Maggie had said *is this yours* and Lenny had said *it's the house's* and they had gone back inside. That was as close as any Rat had come to the Henderson foyer. Lenny was careful about it — the carefulness of a boy who had done the math on what it would cost him in the Corridor if it were known, and who had decided that the Corridor was the first thing in his life he had chosen, and who was not going to let Maple Street take it from him too.

"What time is Hagan home," Maggie said without looking up.

"I heard four."

"His mom letting anyone see him."

"His mom is not letting anyone see him. His mom is mad at the trails, at the Yamaha, at Kevin, at the transformer, and at the state of Massachusetts for building a dirt road behind her house."

Maggie laughed without moving. "Tell him to call me."

"He can't hold a phone, Mag. He broke his collarbone."

"He's got another arm."

Lenny smiled. He hadn't smiled in twenty minutes. "I'll tell him."

The fire alarm at the far end of the Corridor was behind a glass panel with a little red hammer attached to a chain. Someone had set it off in December and nobody had ever proved it. The kids in the Corridor knew who it had been. The kids in the Corridor were not going to say. Lenny let smoke out toward the glass square he had fogged before, and the smoke moved into the sunbeam, and Camus lay open on his thigh at a page he had stopped reading because the sentence had been good enough that he wanted to hold it for a minute before he moved on.

Raised platform. Fourth period. Lunch A.

The Rampers' tables were eight inches above the main floor on a section of poured concrete some architect in 1960 had thought would be used for public speaking and which had immediately and without discussion become the platform. Six long tables. Folding chairs. A sight line of the whole cafeteria that nobody on the platform used except to check whether the hot lunch line was long.

Jackie sat at the second table from the wall with his brown bag open in front of him. Inside the bag — his mother had packed it at six-fifteen that morning with a Styrofoam cup of Tab in the freezer from last night so it would stay cold — was a chicken salad sandwich on wheat bread with the crusts cut off, a peeled orange in a sandwich baggie segment by segment, and two Pepperidge Farm Milanos in a napkin folded into a tight square. His mother was like that. His mother would be like that forever.

Kathy Bellenghi was three chairs down, showing her day planner to a sophomore named Brooke, saying *the Junior Prom is literally six weeks away*, which was the third time in the lunch period she had used the word literally incorrectly and the fourth time today, and Jackie had started to count out of fondness more than irritation. Kathy was fine. Kathy's highlighters were lined up on the formica in the order of the colors of the rainbow, a pencil case with a zipper in the shape of a basketball open beside them. She was filling in a square on the sixth of May with a pink marker. The prom.

Across from Jackie, Donnie Rossi was eating a meatball sub. Donnie had played three sports this year — soccer in the fall, basketball in the winter, baseball this spring — and carried in his right hand the knuckle-scrape of somebody who had slid headfirst on Feeley's mud on Wednesday. The meatball sub came from the deli his uncle ran off Concord Road and had been wrapped in white butcher paper that was by now saturated with sauce and sitting on an open section of the *Boston Globe* sports page so the sauce wouldn't stain the formica. He ate fast. Donnie did everything fast. His dress shirt had been ironed on Sunday night by a mother who woke up at five-thirty six days a week to work the breakfast shift at the Friendly's on Route 20, and by Friday the shirt was a different object from the one that had come off the board — cuff-rolled, collar limp, a stripe of sauce at the second button.

"So, Doctor," Donnie said. He called Jackie Doctor. He had called him Doctor since the first week of September, and Jackie had stopped trying to make him stop. "What's the answer."

"The answer to what."

"To: am I gonna ace the calc quiz sixth period."

"Did you study."

"I studied enough."

"Then you're gonna do fine."

"That's a non-answer. I'm asking an expert. Give me an expert opinion."

Jackie set down his sandwich. He looked at Donnie across the table. Donnie's face was open and amused, the mouth full, the fork of his free hand holding a meatball in the air like a thrown-in question mark. "Expert opinion," Jackie said. "You're gonna get a B-minus and you're gonna tell your mother you got a B-plus and she's gonna know you're lying but not make you take it back because she wants you to feel good about it."

"See," Donnie said to Kathy, who wasn't listening. "See, this is why I talk to the Doctor. He knows my mother."

"Everybody knows your mother, Donnie," Kathy said without looking up from the day planner. "Your mother works the counter at Friendly's. I had pancakes from your mother's hand on Sunday morning."

"And were they good pancakes."

"They were fantastic pancakes."

"That's all I need to hear."

He went back to the sub. Jackie watched him for a beat longer than he meant to. Donnie's right cuff had sauce on it now too. Donnie's mother would wash it tonight when she got home from the four-to-close, and it would be back in the hamper by Sunday night, and on the board by Monday morning, and Donnie would put it on with his eyes half-closed the way any kid puts on a Monday shirt. Donnie was going to apply to UMass Amherst and get in and be the first in his family to go, and none of the kids on this platform would register that as a particular fact because everyone on this platform was going somewhere and the particularity of *first* was not a language this platform spoke.

David Bellenghi was at Jackie's right. David was reading aloud from the Junior Prom ticket that had been mimeographed and handed out in homeroom, reading the part that said *semi-formal*, and laughing.

"Semi-formal means what, exactly," David said.

"Means you can wear your father's tie," Donnie said.

"I don't own a tie."

"You can wear my father's tie," Donnie said. "He's got three. One of them's paisley. You'll look like a lounge act but you'll be in regulation."

David laughed. Kathy did too, absently. Jackie did a small thing with his mouth that was the piano kid's version of a laugh.

Below the platform, at the milk coolers, a girl in mud-brown jeans and a red-checked flannel that was three sizes too big for her — a brother's flannel, the cuffs rolled to her wrists, the hem at her thighs — was lifting a half-pint of whole milk out of the case. A flute case was tucked under her elbow. Her hair was the color of wheat and uncombed at the back, and she was not looking at anyone. Patty Lally had a folded dollar in her other hand and she paid the cafeteria lady and turned and walked with the milk toward the side door that went to the music practice rooms, and she was gone before she could have been expected to have registered on anyone. Jackie's eye tracked her for two seconds as she went, and then he was back to Donnie, and Donnie had said something else that had made Kathy laugh, and the platform went on being the platform.

The bell that ended lunch A would ring in four minutes. A sophomore at the far end of the table was running a highlighter along a sentence in a history textbook. Kathy capped her pink marker. Donnie balled up his butcher paper with the sauce-stained *Globe* sports page inside it and carried the bundle to the trash can in a single walking motion, and on his way back he flicked the back of Jackie's neck with a forefinger as a hello and as a goodbye, and Jackie did not move.

---

Friendly's on Route 20. Friday evening. Eight-fifteen.

The grill was going. The Chef's Special — a double burger with bacon and cheese — was laid out in a row on the griddle, and Eddie the night cook was flipping them in the rhythm he had been flipping them in since 1968. The ice cream case at the front ran the length of the counter, its glass tops fogged at the edges, the mint chocolate chip gone a little bristled where the scoop had taken it down and the case had cycled through a defrost. The red Naugahyde booths ran along the window side, worn smooth at the corners where three thousand kids had slid in and out on their hips over the years. The place smelled like fryer oil and coffee that was forty minutes off the burner and the clean-cold smell of ice cream.

Grace had been on since four. She had twenty minutes left on her feet before Peggy came in for close. Her polyester uniform was tan and brown with a white apron, and the apron pockets were full of the things a pocket collected over a shift — Sweet 'N Low packets, sugar packets, the little folded green guest checks with the carbon copies still attached, two pens, a rubber band, a matchbook from the Wayside Inn she had picked up off a table an hour ago. A pencil was behind her ear. The name tag over her left breast said GRACE in the same typeface they had used since Eisenhower.

At stool four, Dr. Kenneth Bellenghi was eating a bowl of chili and reading the op-ed page of the *Globe* with one hand holding the paper flat against the counter. He was a dermatologist. He had been coming to this Friendly's most Fridays for eleven years because his wife did tennis round-robins on Friday nights at the Sudbury Country Club and the house was empty until nine. He took his coffee black. Grace poured without asking. He said *thanks Grace* without looking up. She said *you're welcome doc* without looking at him. They had been doing this since 1966.

At stool five, one stool away, Mickey Rossi was eating a fried-clam plate. Mickey was the foreman at the sheet-metal shop on Boston Post Road. He had on a flannel shirt and a canvas jacket and his hands were heavy and clean from the work sink and he was reading the sports page of the *Herald* because the *Globe* took the Red Sox too seriously. His coffee was coffee regular — two sugars and cream. Grace poured the refill without asking. Mickey said *thanks hon* without looking up. Mickey's wife Jeanne was working the four-to-close on the other end of the counter, at the register, ringing out a family of five and handing the mother three paper place mats folded in thirds because the youngest kid had asked. Mickey and Jeanne did not look at each other at Friendly's. They had a system. They had had it for twenty years.

In booth two, Donna Henderson — Lenny's mother, though nobody at Friendly's knew the kid — was sitting alone with a Fribble, the second of the week. She was forty-one and recently on her own and she had stopped at Friendly's because the kitchen at home was too bright at eight in the evening and she had not yet figured out how to be in it between the sunset and the eleven o'clock news. The lab at Raytheon had let her go at four. She had driven for twenty minutes without picking a direction and had pulled in because the sign was lit. She had a paperback in her purse she was not reading. Grace brought her a fresh glass of ice water and a straw without being asked.

In booth four, the Carvajal family — mother, father, two kids under ten, a baby in a plastic carrier on the bench — was eating Happy Endings sundaes and arguing gently about who had gotten the extra cherry. The father worked at the Raytheon on Hartwell Avenue. The mother packed lunches for three. The kids had Fribble mustaches. Grace had brought them their check five minutes ago and would bring them a handful of the little red-wrapped mints with the coffee if the father ordered coffee, which he would.

Grace moved along the counter. She refilled Bellenghi's cup. She refilled Rossi's cup. She smiled at the Carvajal kids — the smile that had one specific watt for children and one for adults and one for drunks coming in off the Post Road at eleven — and she slid a clean Fribble water in front of Donna Henderson and took the empty away and said *you let me know when you want another* and Donna Henderson said *Grace you are a saint* and Grace said *not yet* and kept moving.

At the end of the counter, below the register, she bent to pull a fresh stack of green guest checks out of the cardboard box on the shelf. Her knees made a small sound she ignored because she had been ignoring it since March. She came back up and set the stack in the apron pocket on top of the old stack. She had a pen in her hand already. She did not know she had picked it up.

Through the plate-glass window, across the lot, a wood-paneled Buick Estate wagon was pulling in beside a '66 Impala whose muffler you could hear through the glass. Grace did not turn her head. The two cars were nothing to her. Two cars in a Friendly's lot at eight-fifteen on a Friday in April, nothing more. In the booth the Carvajal father lifted his hand for coffee and Grace was already moving toward the pot, and the pencil behind her ear stayed where it was, and the green checks in her apron pocket shifted against her hip as she walked, and outside on Route 20 a kid on a bicycle went past with one hand on the grip and the other holding a white paper bag from Store 24 against his chest, and the bag crackled, and was gone.

**END CHAPTER 11A**

The night they found the chord, Nick couldn't sleep.

Cabin 7 had gone quiet by eleven the way it always did—eight other boys in their bunks, breath settling into the loose unison of camp fatigue, the pine-board walls ticking as the day's heat let go of the metal roof. Somewhere out past the reservoir a whip-poor-will was calling its own name on repeat, patient and mechanical, the way it does for two hours at a stretch until you stop noticing and then start noticing again. A bullfrog answered from the reedy end of the lake. Someone—Cabin 9 or Cabin 10, too far to tell—was playing a guitar under a blanket, the chords muffled and thumb-shaped, a kid trying to finger-pick "Blackbird" and getting most of it right. Outside the screen, fireflies worked the tall grass in slow, distracted pulses.

The boy two bunks down from Nick snored like a tractor. Not like a snore. Like a tractor—the low hitch and diesel catch of an engine trying to turn over in cold weather, once, twice, then the long roll.

"You awake?" Jackie's voice came down from the bunk across the aisle, pitched so it wouldn't carry over the tractor.

"Yeah."

A pause. Then Jackie said, "There's sheet music in our attic."

Nick rolled onto his side so he was facing the voice. "Yours?"

"My father's. Boxes of it. Piano." The word landed with the weight of a thing Jackie had not said out loud before. "I found it last year looking for skis. He doesn't know I saw."

"He played?"

"He played." Jackie was quiet a minute. "He doesn't anymore. The Baldwin in the den hasn't been tuned since before I was born."

Nick thought about that. About Dr. Marsh coming home from the hospital at seven and reading a journal in the wing chair and not looking at the piano that sat in the same room with him. About the sheet music in its boxes, upstairs, getting colder every winter.

"My dad's got a guitar in the garage," Nick said. "In his toolbox. I'm not supposed to know."

"You opened it?"

"No."

The tractor-boy snored. The whip-poor-will kept its count.

"I don't know what I'm going to do after high school," Nick said. It came out before he'd decided to say it, which was how most of the true things he'd ever said had come out. "I don't know if I can do anything."

"You can play."

"Yeah."

"That's something."

"Is it?"

Jackie didn't answer right away. The kid with the blanket guitar had moved on to something Nick didn't know—a slow descending line, almost a lullaby, the low E string buzzing a little where it needed a new set.

"It's what we've got," Jackie said finally.

Somewhere out beyond Cabin 7 the lake did whatever lakes do at midnight. The screen door of the counselors' cabin banged once and didn't bang again. Nick lay on his back and listened to eight other boys breathing and the whip-poor-will counting and his best friend not sleeping.

He thought about Patty's E on top of the triad. He thought about her hands.

He was asleep before he could think about anything else.

February 1980. A Wednesday afternoon. The practice room was on the fourth floor, one window, and the window looked onto West 66th Street. The glass was cold and the sky behind it was the color of unwashed tin. It was not snowing and it was not not snowing — some gray suspended thing was moving past the window without committing.

The Steinway was the one he had loved in September. He had played it enough by now that his hands knew the key-dip was two millimeters deeper than the upright at home, and his wrist set itself for the depth before his fingers thought about it. The lid was open on the full stick. The sheet music was open on the rack — Debussy, *Préludes* Book I, No. 6, *Des pas sur la neige* — in the edition with his own pencil markings from December in the margins.

He was supposed to be practicing Debussy. He had been supposed to be practicing Debussy for the last fifty-three minutes. He had played nothing for the last thirty-one.

He sat on the bench. His hands rested on his thighs. His back was straight. His feet were flat under the pedals. He was not slouched and he was not rigid. He was the shape a man makes when the body remembers a posture the mind has stopped supervising.

The radiator clicked — small metal argument with itself, cough and settle. In the hallway a cellist ran a passage, Schumann, the same four bars, then the same four bars slower, then the same four bars again. Somebody laughed in the stairwell, a young woman's laugh, unembarrassed, and then the stairwell door closed. The practice rooms were soundproofed. Every sound arrived to him the way sound arrives to a swimmer under the surface of a pool.

His hands did not move. He had slept the night before. He was not tired in any way he could have named. The bench was narrow and his weight was distributed evenly on the wood and the wood did not complain.

The clock above the door read 2:47. When he had come in, it had read 1:54. He did not remember stopping. He remembered finishing a phrase and lifting his hands from the keyboard to rest them on his thighs, the way he had been taught to rest them between sections, and he remembered beginning to count the beat, and he remembered losing the count somewhere after three.

Down on West 66th a taxi horn sounded once. A woman in the street was calling a dog. The radiator clicked. The cellist in the hall began the Schumann again. The Steinway's lid reflected the ceiling light in a long black smear.

After a while — he could not have said how long — his right hand lifted from his thigh. It did not lift because he lifted it. It lifted the way a hand lifts from a table when someone calls you from the next room and you are already rising before you have decided. It moved across the air over the keys and came down on middle C without pressing. The pad of the finger rested on the ivory. The key did not move. The string did not sound.

The hand rested there. Half a beat. Two beats. The radiator clicked.

Then the weight came down and the C sounded, clean and warm, the exact C of a Steinway Model B on a fourth-floor afternoon in mid-February, and his left hand came up to meet it, and *Des pas sur la neige* began the way it always began — slow, the tread of a figure over snow. He played it through. He played it perfectly. He played it with care and precision and no visible effort. The last pianissimo settled into the pedal and he held it the length Debussy asked for and he lifted his foot.

He closed the lid. He gathered the sheet music. He walked out. In the hallway the cellist had moved on to a different passage. Somebody at the far end was laughing again.

It will move across the air over the keys and come down on the D above middle C without pressing — the pad of the finger resting on the ivory, the key not moving, the string not sounding. A beat. Two beats. Then his left hand will come up to meet it. The weight will come down. The D minor chord will sound, just the chord, just once — and he will nod, very slightly, the way people nod when they finally hear somebody say out loud the thing they had decided they were alone with.

I don't know him. I have never met him. I am making him up in a Volvo in an empty parking lot at one-twenty in the morning because I need to. He might be out there. He might not. The imagining is what I have.

STUDIO C, the door says, in stenciled letters older than anything the new tenant is planning to do with this frequency. The door is open. Four boxes are stacked in the hall beside it, labeled STUDIO C — EQUIPMENT in the same black marker that labeled everything else, as if the movers couldn't be bothered to distinguish a room from a room.

I have not been inside this room since May 16, 1979. Three twenty-five AM, give or take. I left it with a cardboard-sleeved reel under my arm and Grace Johnson idling in a station wagon in the lot and the two kids who made the tape standing in the doorway where I am standing now.

I stop. I do not go in.

Nine by twelve. I measured it once. Nine by twelve feet exactly, the smaller of the two demo studios in 1979 and a storage closet since the mid-nineties, which is what anybody will tell you if you ask. Nobody will tell you it was anything else.

The acoustic panels are piled in the far corner. Someone has unscrewed them from the walls for the move-out and stacked them the way you'd stack old mattresses, the quilted fabric going grey-brown where thirty years of dust have settled into the weave. On the walls they left behind is the original 1968 plaster, the color of old butter, and on the plaster are the clean shadow-rectangles where each panel used to sit. Clean patches on dirty plaster, the shapes of things that used to matter.

The Yamaha U3 is gone. Sold at auction in '91 or '92 — an engineer told me once at a wrap party, offhand, the way you mention the weather. On the linoleum where it sat there are four small rectangular marks in the floor, one at each leg, pressed into the tile by the piano's own weight over twenty-three years. Four small rectangles in a pattern I could draw in my sleep.

I look at them.

I do not cry. I do not make a sound. I close my eyes for two beats and open them, and the room stays what it is — a storage closet with its storage stripped, a piano-shaped ghost on the floor, a folding chair nobody put away.

The chair sits facing the doorway. Aluminum, the kind the custodian used to drag in when a third person came to a session. Somebody took a break here and did not come back for it.

The boom stands are gone. The DI box off the floor is gone. The control-room glass past the panels is still there, smudged, the control room beyond it stripped to bare conduit.

For three seconds I let myself have it. The D minor chord Jackie's hands found on the Yamaha at two-fourteen AM, thirty years and seventeen weeks ago. Just the one chord. Not the whole song. My memory has always let me have it and has never let me have more.

A janitor passes me in the hall with a mop bucket, younger than my daughter would have been if I'd had one, the casters squeaking on the linoleum. "You doing okay, ma'am." He does not stop.

"Fine. Thank you."

He does not stop.

I stand another beat in the doorway. One step and I am across the sill. I do not take it. Crossing the sill tonight would break something I am not prepared to break. The broadcast is still to come.

I keep walking.

At ten-seventeen the kitchen clock made the small mechanical click it made at every minute, and Eileen Marsh, at the white Formica counter with a damp cloth in her hand, heard it and did not look up.

The counter was already clean. She had wiped it at nine and again at nine-forty-five, and now she was wiping it a third time, a slow circle from the base of the cast-iron trivet to the foot of the cookie jar and back. The cloth left a thin wet arc that dried inside a second. Cleaning a kitchen that did not need cleaning was one of the two or three actions available to a woman of her age and her street when something had to be done and could not be named, and she had put the other two down a long time ago.

Upstairs, through the ceiling and the hallway runner and the door of Jackson's room, the Nocturne came down into the kitchen the way it always came down — soft, a long line of andante, the E-flat opening and the right-hand lift. She heard him play a measure. He paused. He played the measure again. He paused. He played it a third time. Always the same measure. She could have named it. She did not name it.

Her hand on the cloth went slower.

From the study, faintly, the sound of Richard's pencil against a stack of BU undergraduate papers, the small periodic tap when he squared a sheet on the desk. He would be at them until eleven-thirty. That was the architecture of a Tuesday evening in April in this house, and the architecture was sound.

Three notes of a Brahms lieder she had not opened her mouth for in public since a Tuesday afternoon in the fall of 1953 came up unasked, from a shelf lower in her throat than she used now. Contralto low. The register she had trained in before her voice had ever been called a voice. She hummed them. Just the three. Her hand at the base of the cookie jar stopped. She held the three notes in her throat the way a person holds a breath underwater, a small bright pressure behind the sternum — and then she caught herself, and the notes ended, and her hand on the cloth began to move again, harder this time, a tight small circle. The cloth was soaked. Water ran down her wrist to the inside of her forearm and she did not notice it.

On the upper shelf of the pantry, behind the two-tier line of Hunt's tomato cans she kept against winter, was a small flat box wrapped in brown paper and tied with butcher's string. She did not look up at it. She knew where it was the way she knew where the silver was.

She wrung the cloth out in the sink. It came out gray and tired. She laid it across the neck of the faucet where it would dry by morning. She filled the copper kettle at the tap, set it on the front burner, and turned the burner to medium. The gas caught with its small blue sigh.

While the kettle heated, she stood at the counter with her hand flat on the Formica. Her wedding band caught the light from the over-sink fixture. Upstairs the measure went by again — not stopped this time, carried through — and the line of the Nocturne moved on into its second phrase and was gone around the bend of the melody.

The kettle whistled. She made the tea in the Spode cup her mother-in-law had given her in 1958. She carried the cup through the dining room and into the living room and set it on the side table beside her armchair. The Patrick Leigh Fermor was open face-down on the cushion where she had left it Sunday. *A Time to Keep Silence.* Page one hundred twenty-four. She had been on that page for three weeks.

She sat. She picked up the book. The tea cooled at her elbow. She did not drink it. She did not turn the page.

From the study the pencil tapped once against the desk.

From upstairs, the Nocturne continued without pause now, moving through the long middle phrase into the return.

At four minutes past eleven her chin came down to her collarbone. The book settled open on her lap, still on page one hundred twenty-four. Above her, above the ceiling, the Chopin was still playing.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Walk This Way — Cloud Agent startup script
# Builds the local Python virtual environments required by the repo's
# stdio MCP servers. Called by Cursor Cloud Agents on fresh VM spin-up.
# Idempotent — safe to re-run.

set -euo pipefail

echo "[setup] Walk This Way Cloud Agent tooling setup starting..."

# Ensure python3.12 with venv is available.
if ! command -v python3 >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "[setup] ERROR: python3 not found in PATH." >&2
  exit 1
fi

PY_VERSION="$(python3 -c 'import sys;print(f"{sys.version_info.major}.{sys.version_info.minor}")')"
echo "[setup] Python $PY_VERSION available."

# MCPs that need a venv with the `mcp` package installed.
# (james_dickey uses stdlib only, no venv required.)
declare -a MCPS=(
  "zz_COMPASS/MCP_Implementations/STEPHEN_KING_MCP"
  "zz_COMPASS/MCP_Implementations/DENNIS_LEHANE_MCP"
  "zz_COMPASS/MCP_Implementations/WalkThisWay_Character_MCP"
)

for dir in "${MCPS[@]}"; do
  if [[ ! -d "$dir" ]]; then
    echo "[setup] WARN: $dir missing, skipping."
    continue
  fi

  if [[ ! -d "$dir/venv" ]]; then
    echo "[setup] Creating venv in $dir ..."
    python3 -m venv "$dir/venv"
  fi

  # Install deps. Prefer requirements.txt if present; otherwise install `mcp`.
  if [[ -f "$dir/requirements.txt" ]]; then
    "$dir/venv/bin/pip" install -q --upgrade pip
    "$dir/venv/bin/pip" install -q -r "$dir/requirements.txt"
  else
    "$dir/venv/bin/pip" install -q --upgrade pip
    "$dir/venv/bin/pip" install -q mcp
  fi

  # Smoke test: the server file must at least compile.
  "$dir/venv/bin/python" -m py_compile "$dir/server.py"
  echo "[setup] OK  $dir"
done

# Verify the filesystem MCP dependency (Node/npx) is available. Not fatal if
# missing — the server will just error on first invocation.
if command -v npx >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "[setup] OK  npx available for @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem"
else
  echo "[setup] WARN: npx not found; filesystem MCP will not work until Node is installed."
fi

echo "[setup] Complete."
