Downstairs, Eileen Marsh went into the small back bedroom she had not invited anyone into since 1966 and closed the door behind her.

The room had a single north window and a floor lamp with a cracked ceramic base she had meant to replace for eleven years. Along the far wall, a deep utility shelf held nine canvases turned to the wall, the backs of their stretcher bars the only thing a visitor could have seen if there had been visitors. The topmost canvas was dated in pencil on its stretcher, *9/23/65*, and she had carried it up from the basement the year she married Richard because she had not yet decided what to do with it and had never since decided. Beside the shelf stood her old easel, the oil stains on the bar the color of winter sunset under forty years of skin cells and dust. Her palette knife lay where she had put it down on the kitchen of a third-floor Huntington Avenue walk-up in the fall of 1959, a week before the acceptance letter from Richard's department chair changed her address for good.

She did not open a canvas. She did not touch the knife. She stood in the middle of the room with her arms loose at her sides and she looked at all of it the way a widow looks at her dead husband's coat closet — an inventory of a life she had agreed to put down, conducted in private so the agreement would hold.

Through the door and up the stairs, the Chopin came to her in fragments. The E-flat opening. The lift into the andante. A measure Jackson played twice. Then a third time. Then the return. The boy was good and the boy had been good for a long time now and she had taught him nothing — she had *given* him nothing she had kept for herself — and still when he played the first phrase of anything lyrical her right hand lifted involuntarily to her sternum as if to press a brush back against a canvas that was not there.

She was forty-six. She had been forty-six for four months. She had stopped painting at twenty-eight, formally — *set it down*, in her own phrasing, a phrase she had used with her mother and once with a professor and never since with anyone — and at twenty-nine she had given birth to Jackson. At thirty-nine to Elizabeth. Between those two children and the years around them she had run Richard's household the way another woman might have run a small institution: billing, scheduling, laundry, his summer research trips, his departmental wives' luncheons, the endless small repairs of a man who could publish on trauma but could not put a button back on a shirt without cutting himself. Richard was a loved man by his children and by his students, and he was a man who required, in the private way that did not appear in papers or in recommendations, almost constant tending. Medication schedules he would not set for himself. Appointment reminders. The two glasses of water before bed she set on his nightstand because if she did not he did not drink them and woke at three in the morning disoriented. The specific plate he preferred on Sundays. The way the pillow had to be on the bed. Eileen ran this small invisible country the way she had once painted — steadily, without fuss, with the same focus she had brought at twenty-one to a window in February with northern light. She had transferred the focus. She had kept the focus. She had only stopped producing the painting.

Upstairs the Chopin broke off on a phrase and resumed.

She crossed to the easel and stood in front of it. She laid her right hand flat on the wood of the bar where the oil stains were, and the hand remembered. It did the small unconscious thing a hand does when it has held a brush for five hundred hours — the thumb lifted, the first two fingertips curled, the pinky steadied against the heel of the palm — and for half a breath she was twenty-two, standing in a narrow Cambridge kitchen with a canvas on the sink counter and the afternoon light coming sideways across a still life she would never finish. The hand stayed there. It did not move.

From the study across the downstairs hall she heard the particular sound Richard made when he was trying to get up from his chair and the chair was not cooperating — the soft grunt, the scrape of the leg against the floorboard, the pause, the second attempt. He would call her in a moment. He did not like being heard calling her; the call would be quiet.

"Eileen?"

She did not answer immediately. The hand was still on the bar. She looked at the nine canvases turned to the wall and she looked at the palette knife and she looked at the easel her hand was flat against, and then she lifted the hand away with the small care a person uses laying down something that did not belong to her in the first place. She turned off the floor lamp. She left the room and closed the door behind her, and her footsteps across the hall were even and unhurried, the footsteps of a woman on her way to the study.

"I'm here," she said. "I'm coming."

CHAPTER 1: NICK'S WORLD — THE GARAGE

Maxanne Sartori drove up to the Johnson house in her powder-blue Karmann Ghia, the car bottoming out twice on potholes the town never fixed on the working-class side of Hop Brook. Sparks kicked off the undercarriage. She didn't care. She'd heard rumors about a kid on Dutton Road — a kid with a voice that could stop you mid-dial-turn, playing in a garage where the sound punched you in the chest before you opened the door.

The Johnson house squatted like it was tired: mustard paint peeling in long strips, gutters sagging, front steps listing to port. The lawn had surrendered to New England months ago, brown grass poking through dirty snow like stubble on a dead man's face. The bones of the house were good — wide clapboard, solid frame, the kind of place built by someone who knew what plumb meant.

From the detached garage came something alive. Distorted power chords hit the cold March air and traveled through the concrete foundation, through the frozen ground, up through the soles of Maxanne's boots and into her chest. She felt it before she heard it.

Grace Johnson answered the door in her Friendly's uniform, polyester clinging to her frame, name tag reading GRACE in that cheerful corporate font that lies about everything. She smelled like fryer oil and coffee and the particular exhaustion of a woman working her second double this week.

She studied Maxanne — bell-bottoms, oversized sunglasses, standing on the cracked front step like a visitor from a planet where people bought clothes that didn't come from the Jordan Marsh clearance rack.

"You're that lady from WBCN. The one who broke Aerosmith."

"Guilty as charged."

"Nick's in the garage." Grace paused. Something crossed her face — the memory of hope. "Don't fill his head with dreams we can't afford."

"Mind if I listen?"

Grace held her gaze a beat longer than comfortable. "He's been at it since school let out. Won't stop until dinner."

Maxanne crossed the yard toward the garage. The sound grew with each step — bass thrum in the frozen dirt, a snare crack that echoed off the neighbor's siding. The garage door hung open six inches at the bottom, enough to see slivers: a bare bulb swinging on its cord, the silhouette of a kid bent over a guitar, four concrete walls holding more noise than they were built for.

She ducked under the door.

Inside, the air was different — warmer, thicker, heavy with sawdust and motor oil and the metallic bite of old concrete. Dan Johnson's tools hung on a pegboard along the back wall, arranged by size. Claw hammers, box wrenches, a socket set with an empty slot where the 9/16ths used to live — the one he'd had in his pocket the November morning the cable snapped. Tucked behind a pipe wrench was a flattened guitar pick, tortoiseshell, worn thin. Below it, barely visible behind a rusted coffee can, the spine of a spiral notebook with staff lines printed on the pages.

Nick Johnson stood in the center of the garage, mid-solo, fingers moving on a pawn-shop guitar held together with electrical tape at the input jack and faith everywhere else. Twenty-five dollars at the Goodwill in Framingham. New strings from Store 24 when he could scrape together four bucks from mowing lawns. The frets were worn smooth in the first position from a year of playing the same progressions until his calluses cracked and bled and hardened into something useful.

Three other kids backed him — Lincoln boys, Maxanne would learn later, from the even-smaller town that shared a high school with Sudbury but not much else. They stopped when they saw her. That teenage terror of being caught caring about something. The music died mid-note like a bird dropping out of flight.

"Don't stop on my account," Maxanne said, settling onto a paint can. "Play it like you mean it."

They traded looks — four boys deciding whether to trust a stranger from actual radio. Nick decided for them. He launched back into "Dream On" with a fury that made the wrenches rattle on their hooks.

"Every time that I look in the mirror," he sang, "all these lines on my face getting clearer..."

His voice cracked on the high notes. The garage walls seemed to lean in. On the pegboard, a claw hammer vibrated against its nail, buzzing at a frequency only the concrete could hear.

Nick's eyes drifted to the tools. The music faltered — half a beat, barely noticeable, the way a runner flinches passing the spot where someone fell. Then his fingers found the riff again and drove it home.

When they finished, nobody moved. The last note hung in the air. Dust motes froze mid-float.

"What's your band called?" Maxanne asked.

Nick shrugged. "Don't have a name yet. We're just... playing."

"You got a demo?"

The other boys looked at Nick. He shook his head. "Can't afford studio time."

Maxanne pulled out her card. WBCN, 104.1 FM.

"Come by the station. We'll find some time."

Nick hesitated. His eyes moved between the card and the tools on the wall.

"Why?" he asked. "Why would you help us?"

Maxanne stood, knees protesting. "Because Steven Tyler played his first gig in a garage not much bigger than this one. The only difference between him and you is somebody opened a door."

She paused at the garage door, looking back at four boys holding instruments the way drowning people hold wreckage. She wanted to say more. She didn't.

Walking back to the Karmann Ghia, she heard the music start again behind her. "Sweet Emotion" — that bass line crawling out of the garage and across the frozen yard like something that refused to stay buried. Four boys with nothing to lose. The sound carried across Dutton Road, past the potholed asphalt and the bare trees, toward Hop Brook, where it died against the far bank.

Maxanne didn't know it yet, but she was about to meet the other half of the equation. Less than a mile away, on the other side of that brook, a boy sat at a Steinway preparing for a recital.

**END CHAPTER 1**

CHAPTER 2: JACKIE'S WORLD — THE GILDED CAGE

Jackie Marsh woke at 6:47 AM — three minutes before his alarm, the way he always did. The walls were painted a color his mother called Dove Gray. The bookshelves held alphabetized volumes he'd actually read. His piano sat in the corner like a judge waiting to render verdict.

Everything had its place. The tuxedo hung pressed on the closet door for tonight's recital. Sheet music stacked in performance order on the piano bench — Chopin, Bach, Debussy, Rachmaninoff, and the Mozart that would close the evening. His guitar — the electric one his father pretended not to know about — was stored in its case under his bed, gathering dust.

He sat up and looked at the framed photo on his nightstand: himself at seven, hands positioned on piano keys, his mother standing behind him with the kind of smile that suggested she'd finally gotten something right. The photo had won a prize in some parenting magazine — Classical Excellence: Nurturing Your Child's Musical Gift. Jackie remembered the photographer making him hold the position for twenty minutes while they adjusted the lighting.

Through his bedroom window he could see toward the other side of Hop Brook — not that he was looking that direction. Not that he was thinking about someone who used to be his friend before high school taught them they belonged in different worlds.

Tonight was the recital. Tonight he would sit in front of his parents' friends and his father's colleagues and play Chopin and Bach and Debussy like he'd been trained to do since he was five. Everyone would applaud politely and tell Dr. Marsh that his son was remarkably talented, and Dr. Marsh would accept the compliments like tributes to his excellent parenting.

And tonight, if he had the courage, Jackie was going to do something that would remind everyone — including himself — that somewhere beneath all this carefully constructed perfection was a kid who still believed Freddie Mercury understood something Mozart never did.

---

The same week Maxanne Sartori discovered Nick Johnson's garage, Dr. Richard Marsh had called the station personally — a rare gesture, since university professors usually delegated such tasks to their secretaries. He wanted to ensure Maxanne understood just how significant his son's recital would be.

"Jackie trained at the New England Conservatory prep division," he'd said, his voice carrying the careful pronunciation of someone who'd worked hard to lose whatever accent he'd grown up with. "He's being considered for early admission to Juilliard."

Maxanne had wanted to decline. Classical recitals were not her beat. But something in Dr. Marsh's voice — a father's pride laced with something that sounded almost like fear — compelled her to agree. Same desperation she'd heard in Grace Johnson's *don't fill his head with dreams we can't afford*. Different words. Same underlying terror that music might ruin a child's future.

---

By seven o'clock that evening, the Marsh house stood transformed. Folding chairs in rows. A rented Steinway grand that cost more than Grace Johnson made in a year. Champagne chilling in silver buckets. The audience was prep school parents and university faculty — the kind of people who applauded with their fingertips and discussed summer houses on the Cape between selections.

The Marsh house sat on the good side of Hop Brook like it had been placed there by a decorator: Colonial perfection, black shutters against white clapboard, a lawn that would be green come spring. You could walk from Nick Johnson's garage to this front door in twelve minutes, but you'd have to cross Hop Brook — and that narrow stream might as well have been the Atlantic.

Jackie stood in the upstairs bathroom, adjusting his bow tie for the third time. His hands were steady. His mind was not. In two hours he could be back in this bathroom, everyone gone, his parents satisfied that he'd performed exactly as expected. Or he could do what he'd been thinking about for weeks, and everything would change.

---

Jackie entered the living room at precisely 7:30 PM in a tuxedo tailored to fit him, seventeen years old but carrying himself like someone who'd been preparing for this moment since birth. He was beautiful in that way that good nutrition and orthodontics and SAT tutors can manufacture. When he sat at the piano, something changed.

He began with Chopin's Nocturne in E-flat major. His fingers found the keys with practiced precision that spoke of thousands of hours, of lessons that started before memory, of parents who considered anything less than excellence a character flaw. The notes flowed like water, technically perfect, each phrase shaped exactly as his teachers had instructed.

Maxanne was watching Jackie's face. Behind the technical perfection he was dying in there — a boy playing someone else's definition of music, speaking someone else's language with flawless pronunciation and no soul.

The audience nodded, already composing the compliments they'd deliver with their champagne. Dr. Marsh sat in the front row, expression carefully neutral, posture radiating satisfaction.

Jackie moved through the program with mechanical excellence. Bach's Goldberg Variations — excerpts only, because even at a private recital you had to consider your audience's attention span. Debussy's "Clair de Lune." Rachmaninoff's Prelude in C-sharp minor.

Each piece was perfect. Each piece was empty.

Between the Rachmaninoff and the final Mozart, Jackie paused. The pause stretched longer than it should have. Dr. Marsh cleared his throat — a warning about proper recital pacing. But Jackie wasn't listening to his father. He was listening to something else.

His fingers found different keys. The opening notes of "Bohemian Rhapsody" emerged from that Steinway like escapees from prison.

The room froze. You could hear pearls clutching themselves.

"Is this the real life?" Jackie sang, his classically trained voice hitting notes that would have made Freddie Mercury proud. "Is this just fantasy?"

His hands moved across the keys with all the technical skill he'd brought to Chopin, but now that precision served something real. His left hand found a bass line that rumbled through the Steinway's frame and into the hardwood floor. His right hand built harmonies that shouldn't have been possible on a solo piano — Mercury's operatic architecture rendered in ivory and wire and eleven years of lessons finally finding their purpose.

He sang. His voice, trained for Schubert lieder and careful projection, broke open. The champagne glasses on the sideboard vibrated. Dr. Marsh's water glass hummed against its coaster. Four minutes and fifty-five seconds, and Jackie Marsh wasn't performing for anyone in that room.

When he finished, no one clapped. No one moved. Two hundred pounds of social order sat on folding chairs and tried to remember how to breathe.

Dr. Marsh was the first to speak. "That was... unexpected."

"That was rock and roll," Maxanne said, standing up because someone needed to. "That was your son showing you who he really is."

Jackie looked at her then — really looked — and Maxanne saw the same thing she'd seen in Nick Johnson's eyes three days earlier.

"You're Maxanne Sartori," he said. "You play real rock and roll."

Maxanne gave him her card — the same one she'd given Nick. "Come by the station. Bring whatever music lives in you."

Jackie took the card. His hands were still shaking. He looked at it, then at Maxanne, then at his father's face — which had rearranged itself into something Jackie had never seen before. Not anger. Not pride. Something older and more complicated. Dr. Marsh's right hand moved in his lap, pinky and ring finger curling inward once against his thumb — an unconscious reach, the shape the hand had made a thousand times on keys decades ago, years before the Baldwin lid had closed for good.

"Thank you," Jackie said. "For understanding."

The other guests murmured. Mrs. Marsh moved through the room offering champagne, deflecting questions, doing what she'd been trained to do when the social order cracked.

Maxanne walked to her car thinking she'd found two boys worth saving. She didn't know she was setting them on a collision course.

**END CHAPTER 2**

CHAPTER 9A: MAXANNE'S DISCOVERY

Three hours and nineteen minutes.

The talent show story settles over the booth like the last note of a song nobody wants to follow. Two thirteen-year-olds in a gymnasium, harmonizing like they'd stumbled onto the frequency the rest of us spend our lives scanning for.

I take a pull of the Pappy. Let the burn settle.

"You want to know how I got here?" I say into the microphone. "Not the booth. Not WBCN. I mean *here* — the woman telling you about two kids whose dreams she helped kill. You want to understand how a person goes from rebel to executioner in six years? You've got to go back further than Sudbury. Further than 1979. You've got to go all the way back to a bar in Allston that smelled like spilled beer and ambition, and a twenty-three-year-old who was stupid enough to believe that talent and conviction were the same thing."

I spin the chair toward the album wall. Third row, left side. My hand finds it without looking — Aerosmith's debut, the blue wings on cream, January '73. The vinyl's in pristine condition because I never let anyone else touch it.

"1973. Twenty-three years old. About to find the real thing for the first time."

The memory takes me like a riptide.

---

Tuesday in January. The kind of cold that makes your teeth hurt and your breath hang in the air like tiny ghosts. I drove my Dodge Dart down Commonwealth Ave — heater worked when it felt like it, which was almost never — heading to a bar on Brighton Ave called the Brickyard because a sound engineer named Paulie DeLuca had cornered me at the station that afternoon and grabbed my arm.

"Maxanne, there's a band playing the Brickyard tonight. You need to hear them."

"What kind of band?"

"The singer moves like he's trying to shake demons off his skin. The guitar player looks like he'd kill you and not lose sleep over it. They sound like what you'd get if the Stones and the Yardbirds had a kid and raised it behind a dumpster."

Paulie had seen ten thousand bands and been impressed by maybe six. So I went.

The Brickyard sat between a laundromat and a sub shop, a narrow room with a ceiling so low the tall guys hunched, a stage the size of a dining room table, and a sound system that had been state-of-the-art around the Eisenhower administration. The floor stuck to your shoes. The bathroom door didn't lock. The neon Budweiser sign in the window buzzed like a dying insect. The room held maybe twenty people. Half of them teenagers with fake IDs and nowhere warmer to go. A woman at the bar read a paperback, unbothered by anything. The bartender — a thick-necked guy named Sal — wiped glasses with a rag dirtier than the glasses.

Then five guys walked onto that postage-stamp stage, and the air in the room changed.

The singer first. Twenty-four, rail-thin, lips that belonged on a different species, hair that looked like it had been in a fight with a light socket and lost. He wrapped his hands around the microphone stand like it was the only thing between him and the floor. Didn't say hello. Didn't introduce the band.

He looked at the guitar player — dark-haired, cheekbones sharp enough to cut glass, eyes that said he'd already seen things he wasn't going to share with you — and nodded.

The guitar player hit the opening riff.

I've spent my whole career trying not to sound like a tent-revival preacher, so I'll just say this: the sound that came off that stage was alive the way a downed power line is alive. Dangerous, electric, throwing sparks into the night and not caring who gets burned.

Steven Tyler sang like a man who'd swallowed fire and was coughing up something beautiful before it consumed him. Joe Perry played guitar like each note was a personal argument he intended to win. The bass player laid down grooves that producers would spend thousands trying to replicate. The drummer kept time like a heartbeat in a chest that was running out of reasons.

They played forty-five minutes. Four people left during the set — the woman with the book, a couple who'd been fighting since I walked in, some kid who probably had a curfew. The rest of us stood with our mouths open like we'd forgotten how jaws worked.

I had my portable Panasonic cassette recorder in my bag. I carried one everywhere — the day I talked my way into WBCN I swore I'd never let a sound I believed in go unrecorded. The tape quality was garbage. Tinny, distorted, the Brickyard's acoustics making everything sound like it was being played inside a coffee can. But underneath the noise you could hear it. The signal underneath the static that said *this is real*.

After the set I walked up to the singer. He leaned against the wall by the emergency exit, smoking a Camel, T-shirt soaked through.

"Maxanne Sartori. WBCN."

He looked at me like I'd told him I was from Neptune. "The radio station?"

"The one where I'm going to play your album tomorrow night."

He stared. Then he smiled — this enormous, disbelieving grin that transformed his face from dangerous to heartbreakingly young. "We have an album. Nobody plays it."

"I'm going to play it."

"You're going to play it."

"On WBCN. Tomorrow. Eleven o'clock. If I can find a copy."

He reached into a duffel bag and handed me a record like it was a relic. "Dream On," he said. "If you're only going to play one, play that."

I took the album and walked out into the January cold, and the air tasted different. Cleaner. Like the frequency had been adjusted and I was hearing the world properly for the first time in my life.

---

The next night I walked into WBCN at ten-fifteen. Charlie Morris, the station manager, was still in his office — unusual for Charlie, who believed the night shift ran itself or it didn't deserve to exist. He had his feet on the desk and a joint between his fingers and looked up at me with the tolerant suspicion of a man who'd built his station on the principle that rules were suggestions.

"You've got that look," he said.

"I found something."

"You always find something."

I put the Aerosmith album on his desk. "Track three."

He studied the cover. Studied me. Dropped the needle.

For four and a half minutes, neither of us breathed. When the piano came in, Charlie closed his eyes. When Steven Tyler's voice hit that open-throated scream, Charlie opened his eyes and looked at me like I'd just told him where they buried the treasure.

"Where'd you find this?"

"A bar in Allston. Tuesday night. Twenty people in the room."

Charlie picked up the album. Turned it over. Pointed at me with the hand holding the joint, ash dropping onto the desk. "This is what we DO, Maxanne. Find the real shit. Play it tonight. Eleven. Full volume."

Eleven o'clock, I dropped the needle on "Dream On" without announcing it, without context, without checking with the program director who'd left at six. Steven Tyler's voice pouring out of radios across greater Boston — into dorm rooms at BU and Northeastern, into apartments in Cambridge and Somerville, into cars on the Pike, into a city that didn't know yet what it was hearing.

The request line lit up before the song ended. Every light on the board, blinking like a switchboard plugged into something too powerful for its wiring. I played it again at midnight. Twice more before my shift ended at two. By Wednesday afternoon, kids walked into record stores asking for the album by name. By Friday, it had sold more copies in Boston than in the rest of the country combined.

That was discovery. A woman with a cassette recorder in a half-empty bar, hearing something true and having the nerve to share it.

---

Three months later, a kid walked into Studio C for his first radio interview. Twenty-three, skinny as a parking meter, leather jacket that had seen better decades, a bandana that looked like he'd stolen it from a gas station mechanic. He sat down across from the microphone and his hands shook — not nerves, exactly, but the vibration of a body that contains more energy than it knows what to do with.

"You're Bruce Springsteen," I said.

"That's what they tell me."

"From New Jersey."

"Asbury Park. Born to be anywhere else." He grinned. Wild. Unpracticed.

I leaned into the mic. "WBCN, 104.1. I'm sitting here with Bruce Springsteen, who just released his debut album, *Greetings from Asbury Park, N.J.* Bruce, welcome to Boston."

And this kid — unknown, unpolished, absolutely electric — leaned into the microphone and said, with the kind of pure unguarded joy that fame will burn out of you before you ever learn to protect it:

"This is my first time on the radio. My mom lives out in California. HI MOM!"

The control room cracked up. I cracked up. And somewhere out in California, a woman probably pressed her hand to her mouth and understood that her son was going to be all right.

That was 1973. The year I found Aerosmith in a bar in Allston and Springsteen walked in off the street with nothing but a guitar and his mother's love. The year WBCN was exactly what a radio station is supposed to be.

---

I open my eyes. 2009. Studio B. The ON AIR sign still pulsing its cardiac red.

The album wall stares back at me. Aerosmith. The Cars. Boston. J. Geils. All discovered within spitting distance of this booth.

"That was what we were," I say into the mic. My voice sounds old to me now. When did that happen? "We didn't market. We discovered. We didn't focus-group a goddamn thing. We listened. We put our ears to the ground and when the ground shook, we told people about it. And the ground shook often enough that we were right more than we were wrong, and the times we were right — the Aerosmith nights, the Springsteen mornings — those were the times that justified everything. Every bad call, every sleepless night, every screaming match with management about playlist freedom. Because we'd found the frequency. We knew what real sounded like."

I pick up the demo tape. Turn it in my hands. *Demo — Nick/Jackie — un-Authorized — March 1979.*

"But that was 1973. Six years later I had changed. The woman who walked into a bar in Allston and recorded a band on a Panasonic cassette — she was still inside me somewhere. Buried under six years of learning how the business really worked. Six years of watching the frequency get jammed by consultants and demographic reports and suits who thought music was a product you could optimize rather than a wild animal you could only hope to set free."

I set the tape down. Gently.

"In 1973, I found Aerosmith and my first instinct was to share them with the world. In 1979, I found Nick Johnson and Jackie Marsh and my first instinct was to figure out how to use them. I told myself I was still discovering. I told myself the Battle of the Bands was about finding talent. But here's what thirty years of insomnia have taught me: you can lie to management, you can lie to your audience, you can even lie to two seventeen-year-old kids who trust you because you're the woman who broke Aerosmith. The one person you can't lie to forever is the woman staring back at you from the dark window of a radio booth at midnight."

Outside, a bus pulls away from the curb on Boylston, its taillights red as the ON AIR sign.

"Six years. From dropping 'Dream On' unauthorized at full volume to designing a Battle of the Bands with corporate sponsors and demographic targets and a tie clause I buried in the fine print because I thought I could engineer reconciliation the way I'd once engineered discovery."

I lean back. The chair creaks like old leather does — tired, holding on.

"But we're getting ahead of ourselves. Before the Battle, before the rules I wrote in the dark, before the meeting where everything turned — first you need to hear what happened to Nick and Jackie after that talent show. How the golden moment tarnished."

I cue "Dream On." The album cut. The piano intro that still sounds like someone praying in a church they're not sure they believe in.

"Because you can't understand the war until you remember the peace. And the peace between those boys was the most real thing I'd encountered in four decades of rock and roll. What happened to it — what we let happen, what I helped happen — is the reason I'm sitting in this booth, burning the last of my borrowed time."

I press play. Steven Tyler's voice fills Studio B, fills the airwaves, fills whatever's left of a city that once believed a sound from a dive bar could change the world.

I close my eyes and let the music say what I can't.

**END CHAPTER 9A**

CHAPTER 18A: THE STATION MEETING

Two hours and forty-one minutes.

Grace Johnson just left a PTA meeting in her Friendly's uniform and told a room full of professionals what they didn't want to hear. Forty-two to eleven. Not even close. I told you that woman had steel in her spine.

I pour another inch of Pappy. Just an inch. I need to be sharp enough to finish this story and drunk enough to tell the truth.

"You know what the difference is between a rebel and a sellout?" I say into the microphone. "About one meeting. One conference room. One moment when you trade what you believe for what they'll approve. You walk in pure and walk out with a company line, and it happens so smooth you don't feel the cut until you're bleeding all over someone else's floor."

I lean back and the chair protests, and I think: I know how it feels.

"The fall of '76. Two and a half years before the Battle of the Bands, six months before I walked out of WBCN for good, a Tuesday morning meeting I thought was going to be about fall programming. Let me tell you about the meeting that changed everything."

---

WBCN's management office sat on the third floor above the studios — a room that had once been somebody's idea of cool and had aged into somebody's idea of a health code violation. The carpet was the color of a bruise, stained with decades of spilled coffee and dropped cigarette ash. The walls held framed gold records from bands the station had broken, hung at angles that suggested whoever mounted them had been in a hurry or half in the bag. Aerosmith. J. Geils. Boston. The Cars. Each frame a trophy for a war we'd already won and were about to surrender.

The conference table was a slab of pressboard that buckled in the middle, covered in ring stains from mugs ten years of people had set down and picked up while they debated what rock and roll owed to its audience. I'd sat at this table when we decided to give Aerosmith their first heavy rotation. I'd sat here when we broke The Cars and the phones rang for three days straight. I'd argued at this table, cursed at this table, once threw a promotional ashtray at Tom Andrews across this table because he wanted to put a jingle between Led Zeppelin and Black Sabbath.

This was where the real work happened.

The meeting started at ten AM. Charlie Morris — station manager, joint-smoker, believer in letting DJs run free — sat at the head, which told me nothing was wrong. But the man sitting to Charlie's right told me everything was wrong.

His name was Gerald Kowalski. New Program Director, hired six weeks earlier from a station in New York. Late thirties, sharp jaw, hair parted with the precision of someone who had never in his life played an instrument or felt the floor shake under a Marshall stack. He wore a suit in a building where nobody wore suits. He carried a leather portfolio the color of money. His shoes were Italian, polished to a shine that reflected the overhead fluorescents like a funhouse mirror.

I hated him on sight, which I'll admit isn't fair. But I've spent my life trusting my instincts about people the same way I trust them about music, and Gerald Kowalski's frequency was static. Pure, manufactured, corporate static. I would be gone from this building in six months. I did not know that yet. He did.

Tom Andrews sat across from me. Tom — at WBCN since '71, who'd broken J. Geils when Peter Wolf was still his overnight DJ roommate, who'd once stayed on the air twenty-seven straight hours during a blizzard because he believed the city needed rock and roll more than it needed sleep. Tom caught my eye and gave me the smallest nod: *I know. Hang on.*

"Let's talk about the future," Kowalski said.

He opened his portfolio and spread papers across the buckled table like a general deploying troops. Charts. Graphs. Demographic breakdowns printed in the kind of typeface that makes everything look scientific and nothing feel human. Columns of numbers, age ranges, household income brackets, pie charts sliced into segments labeled 18–24, 25–34, Male, Female, College-Educated, Blue-Collar.

"WBCN's core audience is aging," he said. "Our 25–34 demo is up seven percent, but our 18–24 — your growth market, your future — is down twelve percent in the last eighteen months. The advertisers who matter — automotive, audio equipment, lifestyle brands — they're buying 18–34. That's where the dollars live."

He tapped a chart like a teacher correcting a student.

"We need to grow the 18–34 demo, or we lose the automotive sponsors. Lose the automotive sponsors, we lose the revenue that keeps this station independent. Lose the independence — " He spread his hands and smiled the kind of smile that knows it's winning. "Well. You all know what's happening to independent radio."

We did. Clear Channel was swallowing FM stations like a python digesting rabbits. One by one, independent voices replaced by automated playlists generated by consultants in offices that had never been within a thousand miles of the bands they programmed. Boston had lost three stations in two years. We all knew the python was circling our building.

Charlie tapped his pen on the table. "Gerald has a proposal."

Kowalski pulled out a single sheet. Clean. Typed. The heading read: WBCN COMMUNITY ENGAGEMENT INITIATIVE — BATTLE OF THE BANDS.

"Regional high school music competition," he said. "WBCN sponsors. We brand it. We market it to schools within a thirty-mile radius of Boston. Kids enter their bands, we provide judges from our DJ roster, winner gets a recording session and airtime exposure. We sell sponsorship packages — Coca-Cola, local car dealerships, Jordan's Furniture — and position WBCN as the station that discovers the next generation of rock talent."

He paused. Looked around the table with the confidence of a man who knows he's selling something people are going to buy.

"It's community engagement that drives 18–34. It's authentic — local kids, local music, local pride. It's sponsorable — brands want to be associated with youth and discovery. And it's repeatable — we build it as an annual franchise that generates revenue every spring."

The silence lasted about four seconds. The time it takes to cross a line you can't uncross.

"Annual franchise," Tom Andrews said. Not a question. A repetition, the way you repeat a diagnosis you're not ready to accept.

"The data supports it." Kowalski tapped his charts. "Stations that run community engagement programming see a fourteen percent lift in target demos within two rating periods. WJLB in Detroit. KROQ in LA. It's proven."

I looked at Tom. Tom looked at me. And in that look was everything: this was where the road forked. This was where WBCN either stayed what it was — a station that found real music and played it at full volume because we believed in it — or became what everything else was becoming. A brand.

I opened my mouth. And what came out surprised me.

"What if we use it to actually find talent?"

The table turned to me.

"Not as a brand exercise," I said. "Not as a demographic play. As what WBCN does. Discovery. We go into these schools and we listen. We send DJs who know the difference between a kid who can play and a kid who can make you feel something. We don't look for the next marketable act — we look for the next real thing. The next Aerosmith playing a bar in Allston that nobody knows about yet."

Tom leaned forward. "Maxanne's right. If we do this — if we put our name on it — it has to be authentic. WBCN discovers talent. That's the brand, Gerald. If this turns into a glorified corporate talent show, we lose the one thing that makes us worth sponsoring in the first place."

Kowalski watched us the way a chess player watches an opponent move exactly where he wants them. "I agree completely," he said.

He agreed. That should have been my first warning. When the man in the suit agrees with the rebels, the rebels just walked into the cage and closed the door behind themselves.

"Discovery. Authenticity. That's exactly the narrative we sell to sponsors. 'WBCN — Where Legends Begin.' We find talent, we give them a platform, sponsors associate their brands with the discovery process. Everybody wins."

Charlie tapped his pen. "So we're doing this?"

"We're doing this," Kowalski said. "First Battle — spring of '79, let's say, gives us the school-year runway. Lincoln-Sudbury Regional High School. I've already reached out to their music teacher, a Bob Wentworth, who's got connections to the local scene. He's enthusiastic. We start regional, prove the model, expand next year." He looked at me. "Maxanne, I want you to judge. You're the face of WBCN discovery. Your credibility makes this real."

My credibility. Like it was a product he could borrow.

"I'll judge," I said. "But I'm writing the rules."

Kowalski's smile didn't waver. "Of course. Tom, you co-draft with Maxanne. Get me something by Friday." He gathered his charts and his portfolio and his Italian shoes and stood. "One more thing. This needs to work. First time, every time. The sponsors are watching. Make it pay."

Make it pay.

He said it the way you'd tell a vending machine to deliver the soda after you've already put in the coins.

The door closed behind him and the room exhaled.

"Well," Charlie said, lighting a joint. "That's the future."

Tom and I sat. The gold records on the wall stared down at us — bands we'd discovered when discovery meant something, when it wasn't a line item in a sponsorship deck.

"We can still make this real, right?" I said. Not to Tom. Not to Charlie. To the room itself, like the walls might answer.

Tom rubbed his eyes. "If we write the rules. If we control who judges. If we keep the sponsors at arm's length and the kids at the center."

"Then we write the rules," I said.

---

I wrote them that night.

Alone in my apartment in Cambridge — a one-bedroom with a fire escape that rattled when trucks passed and a kitchen window that looked out on a brick wall close enough to touch. I sat at my kitchen table with a legal pad and a bottle of red wine and wrote the rules for WBCN's first Battle of the Bands like I was drafting a treaty between two countries that didn't know they were at war.

Entry requirements. Judging criteria — originality, emotional connection, technical ability, stage presence, with originality and emotional connection weighted double. Prize structure — five hundred dollars to the winner, and a recording session at WBCN's Studio C for the winner and any runner-up.

And then I got to Article 7, Section 3.

I poured more wine.

Article 7, Section 3: "In the event of a tie in the final round, all tied contestants shall share the studio recording session equally, collaborating on material of their choosing, to demonstrate the spirit of musical cooperation that WBCN's Battle of the Bands is designed to foster."

I read it back. Clean, legal, boring. The kind of clause nobody reads in a rules packet. Boilerplate. Standard contest legalese.

Except it wasn't.

I'd already heard the rumors. Two kids from Sudbury — one working-class, one wealthy, once best friends, now enemies — both entering the Battle. Nick Johnson, the guitar kid from Dutton Road with the dead father's garage and the sound that could pull tears out of people who didn't know they were sad. Jackie Marsh, the classically trained prodigy from Maple Street with the Queen belt buckle and the rock and roll heart trapped inside a Juilliard application.

I'd already visited both of them. Already heard what they could do separately. Already imagined — the way you imagine a song before you write it, hearing the ghost of the melody before a single note is played — what they could do together.

The tie clause wasn't boilerplate. It was an ambush. A carefully engineered piece of fine print designed to force two estranged friends into the same recording studio, because I'd convinced myself that if they played together one more time, they'd remember. They'd hear the frequency they'd lost. They'd find their way back to the harmony that had made a middle school gymnasium stand on its feet four years earlier.

I was engineering reconciliation the way Kowalski engineered demographics. Using rules and structures to produce an outcome I'd already decided was right. Convinced that because my intentions were good — because I wanted those boys to make music together — the manipulation was justified. Noble, even.

I finished the wine. Slid the legal pad across the table and stared at Article 7, Section 3.

"It's just a contingency," I said to my empty kitchen. "Standard contest procedure. Ties happen."

Ties happen. Right. And lightning happens, and asteroids happen, and sometimes the thing you've been hoping for your entire career just falls into your lap. Except this wasn't going to fall. I was going to push it. I was going to score those boys close enough that the tie clause would trigger, and then I was going to put them in a room and lock the door and call it opportunity.

Because I believed — genuinely, desperately, with every molecule of the woman who'd walked into the Brickyard in 1973 and heard a sound that changed her life — that Nick Johnson and Jackie Marsh belonged together. That their separation was a crime against music. That if the world wasn't going to fix this, Maxanne Sartori would.

I turned off the kitchen light. Went to bed. Slept the kind of sleep you only get when you've told yourself a lie you really need to believe.

2009. Studio B. My hands around the demo tape.

"That was the meeting," I say into the microphone. "Fall of '76. The day WBCN officially became a business instead of a movement. I turn the tape in my hands. The label in my block lettering. Evidence.

"And that night, alone in my kitchen, I wrote the trap. Dressed it up as a contest rule. Told myself it was boilerplate when it was a loaded gun. "We're not. The rules are already written. The cage is already built. And the lock — the lock clicks so quiet you don't hear it until you're already inside."

CHAPTER 23A: PATTY'S DECISION

The rooster didn't crow at the Lally place. The pigs handled that — two hundred and sixty Yorkshires grunting their way to consciousness at five-fifteen every morning, a sound like the earth clearing its throat.

Patty Lally pulled on her boots at the back door and stepped into April air thick with the smell of hog waste and wet hay. The southeast corner of Sudbury didn't wake up pretty. It woke up honest.

She'd done morning feed since she was twelve. Five-gallon buckets of grain mixed with kitchen scraps, distributed across eight pens while her father checked water lines and her mother tallied receipts at the kitchen table. The pigs pressed against the gates when they saw her coming — not affection, just hunger wearing a familiar face. Patty didn't mind. There was something clean about a relationship that never pretended to be more than it was.

The Cavicchio farm sprawled three fields east, and when the wind came from that direction the combined stench of two pig operations could stop traffic on Landham Road. People on the west side of Hop Brook called it the smell of Southeast. They meant it as an insult. Patty wore it like a badge.

By seven-forty she'd showered twice, braided her hair still damp, and caught the bus at the corner of Morse and Landham. The shower never fully killed the smell. Soap could mask pig but not erase it. She'd learned this in seventh grade when Cheryl Mancini wrinkled her nose in homeroom and said, loud enough for everyone, "Something smells like bacon." The class laughed. Patty didn't. She looked at Cheryl until the laughter died, and said, "Bacon pays our mortgage." Nobody brought it up again.

Lincoln-Sudbury in April smelled like chalk dust and floor wax and the low-grade panic of seniors counting down to graduation. Patty walked the east hallway toward first period, past lockers tagged with band names and Aerosmith vs. Queen graffiti that the janitor scrubbed off every Friday and that reappeared every Monday, the argument as permanent as the cinder blocks underneath.

She stopped at Mr. Wentworth's music room to drop off a permission slip. The room occupied a corner of the building where acoustics went to die — cinder block walls painted institution green, fluorescent lights buzzing overhead, instrument lockers that smelled like valve oil and teenage spit. But on the corkboard between a yellowed Boston Symphony schedule and a jazz band sign-up sheet that nobody had signed, someone had pinned something new.

Block letters on goldenrod paper.

BATTLE OF THE BANDS
MAY 15, 1979
LINCOLN-SUDBURY REGIONAL HIGH SCHOOL
GRAND PRIZE: $500 AND PROFESSIONAL RECORDING SESSION
SPONSORED BY WBCN "THE ROCK OF BOSTON"

Patty read it twice. Not the prize money — five hundred dollars wouldn't change what she already knew about her music. She read the date. Six weeks away. Six weeks to decide whether she wanted to walk into a war zone carrying a guitar instead of a weapon.

---

She'd been watching them for months.

The cafeteria at Lincoln-Sudbury split like a cell dividing — Nick Johnson's table near the windows where the Rollers and working-class kids ate fast and loud, Jackie Marsh's table by the doors where Rampers debated college applications over sandwiches their mothers had wrapped in wax paper. Between them, thirty feet of linoleum they did not cross.

Patty sat with Kristy Wesslen and Robin Bosshard at a table near the milk coolers — neutral ground, neither camp, claimed by nobody. From there she could see both boys without turning her head. Nick hunched over a tray, jaw working, not talking much, eating the way a man fuels machinery. Jackie sat with posture like a conductor waiting for the downbeat, every gesture measured, every word selected before it left his mouth.

Two boys performing different versions of who they thought they had to be.

The strange thing was the way they never looked at each other. Not avoiding. Avoiding would require acknowledgment. This was something worse. They'd erased each other from the room. Nick's eyes swept the cafeteria and skipped Jackie's table like a scratch on a record, the needle jumping over the part it couldn't play. Jackie's gaze moved through the space where Nick sat as if that corner of the cafeteria held nothing but empty chairs.

Patty saw it because she remembered when they couldn't stop looking at each other.

---

Camp Elbanobscot. Summer of 1975. A music camp tucked into thirty acres of pine and scrub oak off Route 117, where Sudbury's conservation land met the river. Fifteen kids, three cabins, a piano that needed tuning, and a counselor named Dave who played Joni Mitchell so well that even the boys shut up and listened.

Patty had arrived knowing no one. Thirteen years old, already tall, her wheat-colored hair hanging straight to her waist, smelling faintly of something the other kids couldn't name but she could. Home. She'd packed extra soap and a bottle of her mother's perfume, just in case.

She didn't need them.

Nick Johnson sat on the dock the first morning, bare feet in the water, playing an acoustic guitar like he was arguing with it. No finesse — his fingers hit the strings hard enough to make them buzz against the frets, and the sound that came out was raw and specific and his own. He played "Dream On" like a boy talking to someone who'd left the room and wouldn't come back.

Jackie Marsh sat at the camp piano in the music cabin, running scales that melted into something from Queen when he thought nobody was listening. The shift happened in his hands — rigid precision loosening into something riskier, wilder, alive. When he played what he wanted instead of what he'd been taught, his shoulders dropped three inches.

On the third day, Dave put all three of them together for a group exercise. "Find harmony," he said. "Not unison. Harmony. Three different notes that need each other."

Nick started singing "Your Song." Elton John — not his usual territory, but the melody was simple enough. His voice cracked on the high notes and he didn't hide it. Jackie came in underneath with piano chords that steadied the song without smothering it. And Patty — Patty found the space between them.

Nick's voice ran hot. Jackie's ran cool. And there was a temperature in the gap between them, a frequency where neither boy lived alone. She stepped into it with her voice and the gap closed.

Dave stopped the exercise. Just stood there with his hands at his sides and his mouth half-open, because what he was hearing shouldn't have come from three kids who'd met three days ago.

"Do that again," he said.

They did it all week. By the lake at sunset. In the music cabin during free period. Walking the trails between sessions, Patty humming the melody while Nick and Jackie found their parts without thinking, three voices braiding until you couldn't hear where one ended and the others began. The pine trees listened. The lake held still. And for five days, nothing in the world mattered except the sound they made when they stopped trying to make it.

Now she sat by the milk coolers in a cafeteria that smelled like industrial ketchup and watched two boys who couldn't even look at each other, and the distance between what they'd been and what they'd become sat in her chest like a stone she'd swallowed years ago and never passed.

---

She brought it up at rehearsal.

St. Michael's Church on a Tuesday evening, the four of them sprawled across pews that smelled like old hymnals and lemon oil. Robin Bosshard sat cross-legged on the altar steps, bass across his lap, his faint Swiss accent making every sentence land a half-beat slower than the words around it. Kristy Wesslen picked at her acoustic, blonde hair curtaining her face. Steve Bankuti tapped a paradiddle on the back of a pew with his sticks — a habit so constant that Patty sometimes heard it in her sleep, ghost rhythms in the dark.

"Battle of the Bands," Patty said. "WBCN's sponsoring it. May fifteenth. Eight slots."

Robin looked up from his bass. "At Lincoln-Sudbury?"

"We'd have to register by Friday."

Kristy stopped picking. "That's the Nick Johnson and Jackie Marsh show. The whole school's chosen sides."

"I know."

Steve's paradiddle stopped. In the sudden silence the church creaked around them — old wood settling, a radiator ticking somewhere in the walls.

"What are you saying?" Steve asked.

"I'm saying we enter."

Robin set his bass down. He did that when he wanted to think, as if the instrument's weight cluttered his head. "Why?"

Patty looked at the stained glass above the altar. St. Michael with his sword, standing over something beaten. Evening light through colored glass threw patches of red and blue across the wooden floor like bruises on the church's skin.

"Because somebody has to play music that isn't a weapon."

Kristy exchanged a look with Steve. "You want to walk into their war?"

"I want to play our songs. 'Dreams.' 'Landslide.' 'Silver Springs.' 'Go Your Own Way.' The way we play them — not louder, not angrier, not more perfect. Just honest."

"And what does that do?" Robin asked. Not skeptical — curious. Robin was always curious. It was his most useful quality and his most infuriating one.

"I don't know," Patty said. "Maybe nothing. Maybe you can't fix something by playing music at it. But I heard what those two sound like in the same room, and right now they've forgotten. Somebody has to remind them."

Robin picked his bass back up, turned it in his hands. "So we're entering a war to play peace songs?"

Patty almost smiled. "Something like that."

Steve resumed his paradiddle — faster now, a double stroke roll that rattled the hymnal rack. "Nick's band plays like they're kicking down a door. Jackie's band sounds like the Boston Pops with better taste in rock. We'll get swallowed."

"I don't care about winning."

"Then what's the point?"

She thought about the lake at Elbanobscot. Three voices and the pine trees and the last light on the water. The way Dave had stood there, frozen, because what he was hearing had no business coming from kids who barely knew each other's last names.

"The point is showing up. The point is playing music that remembers what music is for."

Kristy started picking — the opening notes of "Dreams," slow and sure. Robin found the bass line without being asked. Steve joined with brushes on the pew back, soft as rain on a window.

Nobody said yes. Nobody had to.

---

She walked home after rehearsal because the bus didn't run past seven and her mother was buried in feed invoices. Two miles through Southeast Sudbury in the April dark, past the Cavicchio property where the security light threw long shadows across empty pens, past the conservation land where mini-bike tracks scarred the trailheads like old wounds, past mailboxes that leaned toward the road like tired men waiting for news that never came.

The smell found her at the property line. Thick, animal, alive. Home.

Other girls at Lincoln-Sudbury fought for their freedom with clothes and attitudes and the careful deployment of cruelty. Patty fought for hers with feed buckets and guitar calluses and the stubborn refusal to be ashamed of where the wind blew from.

She wasn't the kid who got invited to parties on the west side of Hop Brook. She wasn't the kid whose mother drove a Volvo to PTA meetings or debated summer programs over white wine in kitchens with granite countertops. She was the kid who could tell the difference between a gilt and a sow by sound alone and didn't apologize for any of it.

The house sat dark except for the kitchen light — a small colonial with vinyl siding that needed paint, a barn that leaned east, and a yard where chickens had beaten the grass into mud. Her mother sat at the table, calculator and ledger open, reading glasses pushed up on her forehead. The radio played something country, turned low enough to be company without being conversation.

"Rehearsal okay?"

"Yeah. We're entering the Battle of the Bands."

Her mother looked up. "At the high school? The one with the radio station?"

"WBCN. Yeah."

A pause. Calculator set down. Glasses removed. The look a mother gives when she knows her daughter is about to walk into something complicated and has decided to let her do it anyway.

"That's the Johnson boy and the Marsh boy's thing. The whole town's been talking about it."

"I know."

"You sure you want to get in the middle of that?"

Patty opened the refrigerator, found last night's meatloaf, and ate it cold over the sink. The meat was dry. She didn't care.

"I'm not getting in the middle of anything. I'm just playing music."

Her mother watched her eat — the expression of a woman who'd raised a daughter to make her own decisions and wasn't about to start second-guessing now, but who reserved the right to worry.

"Okay," she said. And went back to her ledger.

---

Friday. Last period. 2:45 PM.

The hallway outside Wentworth's room had cleared. Most kids were already gone — sprinting for buses, idling in parking lots, scattering into the warm afternoon like seeds from a dandelion head.

Patty walked into the music room alone. The fluorescent lights hummed their one flat note. Wentworth sat behind his desk grading papers with the patience of a man who'd traded symphony halls for steady paychecks twenty years ago and had mostly stopped regretting it.

The sign-up sheet for the Battle of the Bands sat at the corner of his desk. Seven names filled the seven lines above the last blank space.

"Mr. Wentworth."

He looked up. Pen still in hand.

"I'd like to register a band."

Something shifted in his face. Not surprise. Recognition. He'd heard Patty sing in music class — had stopped mid-sentence once, the way Dave had stopped at camp, because the voice coming out of this tall girl from the pig farms wasn't the voice of a girl who should have been sitting in a high school music class filling out worksheets about time signatures.

"Band name?"

"Rumours."

He wrote it down. Careful block letters.

"Members?"

"Robin Bosshard on bass and guitar. Kristy Wesslen, harmonies and acoustic. Steve Bankuti, drums. Me on lead vocals and guitar."

"Genre?"

"Fleetwood Mac."

Wentworth set his pen down. Leaned back. Studied her — this girl with damp-braided hair and fingers callused from steel strings and the faintest trace of something soap couldn't conquer.

"You know what you're walking into," he said.

It wasn't a question.

"I know what I'm walking into."

He held her gaze for a moment longer, then slid the registration form across the desk. "Eight bands. You're the last slot."

Patty signed her name. The pen scratched against the paper, loud in the empty room.

She took the carbon copy, folded it into her back pocket, and walked out into the hallway. The fluorescent lights buzzed overhead like trapped insects. The linoleum gleamed under her boots. Somewhere down the corridor, a locker slammed — the last student, the last echo, the building settling into the hollow quiet of a Friday afternoon.

Six weeks.

She hummed "Go Your Own Way" all the way to the bus stop. Not as a statement. Just something she did.

CHAPTER 23B: PATTY'S PREPARATION

St. Michael's smelled like dust and devotion and whatever they put in the wood polish that made the pews glow amber under the overhead lights.

Patty had arranged the rehearsal for Tuesday — five o'clock, after the parish secretary locked up and left the key under the mat because Father DiNardo trusted musicians the way he trusted anyone who brought their own instrument to a house of God. The church was theirs from five to eight, and by five-fifteen they'd moved hymnals off the front pews, run an extension cord from the sacristy outlet, and turned the altar into a stage.

Steve set up his kit on the altar rug — snare, hi-hat, kick drum, a ride cymbal he'd bought at a yard sale in Maynard for three dollars. Robin plugged his bass into a small Fender amp wedged between the pulpit and the baptismal font. Kristy perched on the communion rail, acoustic guitar across her knees, tuning by ear because the electronic tuner Steve had borrowed from his older brother ate batteries faster than it found notes.

Patty stood at the center, where the priest stood on Sundays. Guitar strap over her shoulder. No setlist written down — she carried it in her head, each song in sequence, each transition mapped to the emotional architecture of what she wanted the audience to feel. Not think. Feel.

"Dreams" first. Open with longing. Let them settle.

"Landslide" second. Slow it down. Make them listen.

"Silver Springs" third. Turn the heat up. Let the ache build.

"Go Your Own Way" to close. Give them back their feet.

She'd chosen every song the way a surgeon chooses instruments — not for spectacle, for function. Each one carried a specific message, and threaded together they formed an argument she couldn't make with words because words had a way of starting fights and she wasn't here to fight.

Nick wouldn't hear it that way. Jackie wouldn't either. That was fine. Patty wasn't playing for their conscious minds. She was playing for the part of them that still remembered a lake, a sunset, three voices braiding in the pine-scented air before the world taught them to be afraid of harmony.

---

"From the top," she said. "Dreams."

Kristy started the intro — that floating C-major arpeggio that Lindsey Buckingham had made sound like falling water. Robin found the bass note underneath, a slow pulse. Steve came in with brushes, barely touching the snare, a whisper rhythm that said: listen.

Patty closed her eyes and sang.

"Now here you go again, you say you want your freedom..."

Her voice rose through the church. Past the pews and the hymnals and the offering boxes. Past the Stations of the Cross and the stained-glass St. Michael with his sword and the plaster saints in their wall niches who'd heard every kind of prayer but this. Up into the vaulted ceiling where the old beams held the weight of a hundred years of worship and the sound bounced back down warm and strange, the church itself becoming an instrument.

By the second verse, Robin had locked in. His bass hummed through the stone floor — you could feel it in your feet, a low vibration that connected the music to the bones of the building. Kristy leaned into the harmony on the chorus, her voice winding around Patty's like ivy around a trellis, different but inseparable. Steve's brushes hissed against the snare with the patience of someone who understood that rhythm wasn't about speed. It was about trust.

They ran "Dreams" three times. The first was loose — finding the tempo, remembering where the dynamics shifted. The second was tighter, the four of them listening to each other with the concentration of people defusing a bomb. The third was the one that mattered. On the third pass, the song stopped being four people playing and became one sound breathing.

"Landslide" came next. Patty alone at first — just voice and acoustic, the pick pattern Stevie Nicks had turned into a kind of lullaby for grown-ups. The church went still. Even Steve put his sticks down. There was no percussion in "Landslide," and Steve was smart enough to know that silence was a drummer's most powerful tool.

"I took my love, I took it down..."

Her voice cracked on the second line. Not a mistake — the crack was the song. Patty didn't smooth it over or pretend it hadn't happened. She leaned into it the way a good carpenter leans into the grain of the wood, letting the flaw become the feature. The congregation of empty pews received it. The saints in their niches received it. The dust motes floating in the evening light through stained glass received it and kept moving, indifferent and beautiful.

They worked for two hours. "Silver Springs" needed the most attention — the build from quiet verse to soaring chorus was the hardest transition, the place where a lesser band would either rush the crescendo or let the quiet parts die of neglect. Patty made them run the bridge eleven times until Robin's bass walk ascended in perfect parallel with her vocal line, two rivers meeting.

"Go Your Own Way" was the easiest. They'd played it a hundred times — at birthday parties, in Kristy's basement, at the Concord River cleanup where the only audience was a dozen volunteers in rubber boots. The song was in their muscles. All they had to do was let it out.

At eight o'clock, they packed up. Steve broke down his kit with the efficient motions of a kid who'd been setting up and tearing down drum sets since he was twelve. Robin coiled cables. Kristy stacked hymnals back into the pew racks.

"That felt different tonight," Robin said, zipping his bass into its case.

"Good different?" Patty asked.

Robin paused. Held the case in both hands. "Intentional different. Like you know something we don't."

Patty turned off the Fender amp. The hum died, and the church filled with the kind of silence that only exists in places built for it.

"I know what I want the music to do," she said. "That's all."

Robin looked at her for a long moment. Then he nodded, once, and walked out into the parking lot where his mother's Buick idled under the security light.

Wednesday. 11:15 AM. The hallway outside the biology lab.

The between-class crush at Lincoln-Sudbury moved like cattle through a chute — four hundred kids in six minutes, shoulder to shoulder, sneakers squeaking on linoleum, the air thick with body spray and bubble gum and the low roar of voices saying nothing important at maximum volume.

Patty pressed against the lockers to let a group of Rampers pass. She had biology in three minutes and the textbook weighed six pounds and her locker combination had been sticking since February.

Nick Johnson came from the other direction. Walking fast, guitar case slung over his shoulder like a rifleman carrying his weapon, head down, the set of his jaw saying don't talk to me and the tension in his shoulders saying I dare you to try. He'd lost weight since she'd last looked at him — cheekbones sharper, eyes darker, the softness of the boy she'd known at Elbanobscot burned away by two years of grief and a house where the mortgage was always a month behind.

He passed within arm's reach.

Patty hummed. Not deliberate — it was something she did, the way other people cracked their knuckles or tapped their fingers. A melody lived in her throat at all times, and the one that surfaced now was "Go Your Own Way." Five notes. The opening phrase. A reflex, not a message.

Nick stopped.

One step past her. Frozen. His shoulders tightened, then loosened, then tightened again — the micro-movements of a body fighting a memory it didn't want to acknowledge. He turned his head, not all the way, just enough to show his profile against the fluorescent light. Something in the melody had caught him. A hook snagged on a memory buried so deep he couldn't name it — a lake, pine trees, a girl's voice finding the space between his and Jackie's, a week when music hadn't been a war.

He looked at Patty. She looked back.

For one second the hallway noise fell away and they stood in the gap between past and present, two people who knew what the other sounded like at thirteen, what their voice did when it wasn't trying to prove anything. The recognition was there — faint, underwater, a shape seen through clouded glass.

Then Nick blinked. Shook his head, a half-motion, like shaking off a chill. He walked on. Guitar case bouncing against his hip. Gone around the corner before Patty could exhale.

She watched him go. The hallway refilled with noise. Lockers slammed. Somebody laughed too loud about something that wasn't funny.

Patty leaned against the cool metal of her locker and let the melody die in her throat. Five notes. She hadn't planned them, hadn't aimed them. But they'd landed.

She hefted her biology textbook and walked to class.

Thursday. 4:30 PM. Wentworth's music room.

Patty had come back for the guitar picks she'd left in the instrument cupboard during last period. The hallway was empty — after-school clubs had migrated to the gym, and the music room existed in the deep quiet that settled over unused classrooms like dust on a shelf.

She opened the door and heard the piano.

Jackie Marsh sat at the upright in the corner. Not the Steinway in the band room — the scarred practice piano that Wentworth kept for students who needed to work through something the Steinway was too pristine to hold. Jackie's back was to the door. His blazer was draped over the piano bench beside him. His sleeves were rolled to his elbows, and his hands moved over the keys with the kind of precision that costs ten thousand dollars in lessons — but something else was happening in the music. Something the lessons hadn't taught.

He was playing "Somebody to Love."

Not performing it. Not rehearsing it. Playing it the way a person writes in a journal — private, unpolished, honest. The runs weren't clean. He let notes ring too long or cut them too short, feeling his way through the song instead of executing it. His left hand found the bass line by instinct, not by chart, and the chord voicings were his own — darker than the original, more complex, stacked with dissonance that resolved into something aching and true.

"Can anybody find me somebody to love?"

He sang it quiet. Barely above the piano's volume. Not Freddie Mercury's operatic howl — Jackie's voice, stripped of the performance polish he wore like armor, raw and reaching, the voice of a boy who meant every word and wished he didn't.

Patty stood in the doorway. She didn't move. Didn't breathe loud enough to break the room's agreement with Jackie's playing — the old walls and the fluorescent lights and the instrument lockers all holding still, offering the boy what the rest of his life refused to give him: a space where he didn't have to be perfect.

The song ended. The last chord hung in the room for three seconds, then two, then one, then gone.

Silence.

"That was real," Patty said.

Jackie spun on the bench. His hands came off the keys like they'd been burned. His eyes went wide — not fear, exactly, but the wild exposure of someone caught without their costume, standing in their own skin for the first time in front of someone who could see them.

"How long have you been standing there?"

"Long enough."

He stared at her. His mouth opened, closed, opened again. She watched the armor rebuilding in real time — shoulders squaring, chin lifting, the careful construction of a boy who'd been taught that vulnerability was a weakness and musicianship was measured in precision, not feeling.

But underneath it, in the second before the walls went up, she saw something she recognized. The same thing she'd seen at Elbanobscot when Jackie played Queen in the music cabin and thought nobody was listening. The same dropping of the shoulders. The same breath.

Patty turned to leave.

"Patty."

She stopped. Looked back over her shoulder.

Jackie sat on the piano bench with his hands in his lap. The armor was up, but it had a crack in it — a thin line running from his throat to his chest where the song still lived.

"What are you doing here?" he asked. The question meant more than the words.

"Getting my picks," she said. "From the cupboard."

He nodded. Not satisfied, but unable to ask what he really wanted to ask.

She crossed the room, opened the instrument cupboard, found her picks in the small cardboard box where she kept them — three medium tortoiseshell Fenders, worn smooth at the tips. She put them in her jacket pocket.

At the door, she stopped again. Not for drama. Because something in her wouldn't let her leave without saying it.

"You don't play like that when anyone's watching."

Jackie said nothing.

"You should."

She walked out. The door closed behind her with a soft click. In the hallway, her boots sounded like a slow heartbeat on the linoleum.

The night before the Battle.

St. Michael's Church. 10 PM. Everyone gone.

Patty sat barefoot on the altar rug. The wool was rough under her feet — decades of knees and spilled communion wine and the slow wear of people kneeling to ask for things they already had. Her guitar sat in her lap. A Martin D-28 her father had bought used from a music shop in Framingham when she was fourteen, the spruce top darkened with age, the neck worn smooth where her thumb rode the back during chord changes.

The church was dark except for the votive candles flickering in their red glass holders near the side altar. Thirty small flames making thirty small shadows that moved on the walls like the ghosts of prayers that hadn't been answered yet.

She didn't play. Not at first. She sat with the guitar and listened to the church breathe — the radiators ticking their cooling rhythm, the old wood popping in its joints, the wind pressing against the stained glass from outside, St. Michael's sword catching the last light from the parking lot in a thin line of amber.

Tomorrow she'd stand on a stage in front of nine hundred people. Nick would be there with his grief and his duct-taped guitar and the fury that passed for music when you couldn't say what you actually felt. Jackie would be there with his precision and his blazer and the voice he only used when he thought no one could hear. Eight bands. A war dressed up as entertainment. A town watching its children fight each other because adults couldn't figure out how to stop drawing lines.

She couldn't save them. She knew that. She'd known it since camp, since the last morning at Elbanobscot when they drove away in different cars toward different lives and she stood on the gravel path with her duffel bag and understood — at thirteen, with the certainty that only children possess — that the world would not make room for what they'd found.

But she could play.

She could stand on that stage and play music that didn't ask for anything — not victory, not vindication, not proof that one kind of life was worth more than another. She could play "Dreams" and mean it. She could play "Landslide" and let her voice crack on the second line because the crack was real and real was the whole point. She could play "Silver Springs" and let the chorus swell until the walls pushed back. She could close with "Go Your Own Way" and let the room decide what that meant.

She placed her fingers on the fretboard. C-major to G. The opening of "Go Your Own Way." The pick caught the low E string and the note filled the church, one clean tone expanding outward through the empty pews and the votive shadows and the stone walls that had heard a century of prayers and confessions and knew the difference between performance and truth.

Patty played it through. Once. The whole song. Alone in St. Michael's with her bare feet on the altar rug and the candles burning down and the wind outside pressing against the colored glass like it wanted to come in and listen.

When the last chord faded, she didn't move. The silence that followed wasn't empty. It was the silence of a room that had received something and was holding it, the way a church holds everything — the grief and the gratitude and the stubborn human insistence that some things are worth singing even when nobody's listening.

She wasn't nervous. She wasn't hopeful. She was ready.

She packed her guitar. Slid on her boots. Blew out the votives one by one — thirty small flames dying between her fingers, thirty small trails of smoke rising toward the ceiling in the dark.

She locked the church door behind her and walked into the May night.

The stars were out. The air smelled like cut grass and lilac and, faintly, from the southeast, the honest smell of home.

She hummed "Go Your Own Way" all the way to her mother's car.

**END CHAPTER 23B**

## Forbidden list (things removed from prior drafts — DO NOT resurrect)

Any future agent must NOT reintroduce any of the following under any circumstances:

- **Original songs written by Nick, Jackie, or Patty.** They are high-school kids in a cover band only. No teen-written lyrics. No "Hop Brook Blues" (a previously cut original with rhyming teen-poetry lyrics). No original Nick compositions on stage at the Battle. No original Jackie-and-Nick song written together in the garage. The Studio C mashup in Ch 32 is the novel's one original moment and it is INSTRUMENTAL — Aerosmith riffs (Sweet Emotion, Walk This Way) folded with Queen harmony (Bohemian Rhapsody). No words written by the boys.
- **A Prologue.** The opening chapter is **Chapter 1: THE LAST VOICE OF BOSTON ROCK, AUGUST 2009** (Maxanne in Studio B). It is not labeled "Prologue" anywhere in this draft.
- **Feb 1980 Juilliard practice-room scene.** Cut per the 1979→2009 window rule. Jackie's final 1979 appearance is the November 1979 WBCN visit to Maxanne.
- **Ch 33 Section III (Maxanne 1982–2009).** Cut per the same window rule.
- **"Comfortably Numb"** as WBCN's corporate-approved final song. It's "Shine On You Crazy Diamond."
- **"Prudential Tower"** as Dan's worksite (the Prudential was completed 1964). Dan dies at 60 State Street.
- **Dr. Marsh as a guitarist.** He is a pianist.
- **"Casio"** as any 1970s-era keyboard. Anachronism (Casio consumer keyboards shipped 1980). Jackie's basement keyboard is a Wurlitzer 200A. Mark Pianka's grandmother's keyboard is a Magnus chord organ.
- **"Lansdowne Street"** as the location of The Rat. The Rat was at 528 Commonwealth in Kenmore Square.
- **"The labyrinth wins / three casualties of the same war / Nick stayed real, Jackie compromised, I fled"** sermon triad. Cut everywhere it tried to appear.
- **"Walk this way, I think. Yeah. Walk this way."** as a title-drop final sentence.
- **"THE END"** at the close of Ch 34 (or wherever the final chapter lands). The novel closes on an image, not a stamp.
- **Any character activity between September 1979 and August 2009.** Maxanne's 1980s–2000s trajectory, Jackie's Juilliard years after his September 1979 arrival, Nick's Army years after his September 1979 ship-out. All cut. If it happens between those dates, it doesn't appear in the novel.
